"A toast to electronic music!"
Echo pops up first, soda raised high.
"A toast to every beating heart."
Inspector stands, too, toasting Triss across the table.
"Then, to celebrate the success of this project—"
"Cheers!!!"

Night shimmers with color.
Glass clinks rise and fall, mingling with the laughter of the young—leaving the perfect footnote on this summer.

"Oh no! We forgot—we should've snapped a picture when we clinked!"
"If we forgot, we forgot. It's fine."
Triss smiles—
"We'll have plenty more parties to celebrate."

"Thank you all for coming!"

Onstage, I looked up at the audience.
The aquarium's open-air stage wasn't exactly small, but it wasn't built for a live show like this, either. Against a tide of devoted fans, it could only do so much. Before long, the place was packed wall to wall.
The summer sun was so bright I could barely keep my eyes open—but that was exactly why the fans who'd stayed and waited for me shone all the brighter.

"And now, please enjoy—"

This was my summer, day in and day out. Buoyed up by everyone, I got to sing my heart out on this little stage above the water.

"A tour at an aquarium?"

When the Inspector first brought it up, I blinked in surprise.

An idol can perform on all kinds of stages.
Theaters, plazas, shopping streets—even makeshift promo stages thrown together on street corners. I'd stood under spotlights, before rain-washed shop windows, wherever fans came out waving their glow sticks.
But an open-air stage at an aquarium—that would be a first.

"Won't it bother the little ones in there?"

"The little ones?"

"The dolphins, the penguins—the jellyfish and all the rest."
"If the music's too loud, wouldn't that upset them?"

Though now that I thought about it… can jellyfish even hear? I was suddenly a little curious.

The Inspector handed me the schedule.

"Don't worry. We've already confirmed everything with the aquarium. We'll keep the volume at a safe level."
"And most importantly, they've promised that all the proceeds from this collaboration will go straight to marine conservation."

Back then, I had no idea that—more than the dolphins or the penguins—the one I'd really need to worry about was an eel. One I'd later find by the edge of the performance pool.

Strictly speaking, though, it wasn't exactly an eel. Electric eels aren't actually true eels, after all.

After the show, backstage was much quieter than the stage had been.
I thanked the crew who'd quietly kept everything running, took the water the Inspector handed me, and was just about to ask whether the aquarium had any new notes for me when a faint sound came from deep in the equipment area.

Splat.
Like something wet had dropped onto the floor.

"Hm? Inspector, did you hear that?"
The Inspector blinked at me, not quite catching on.

The workroom, normally a break space for the dolphin and orca trainers, was packed now with stage crew and sound gear, everyone too busy to notice what was going on in this little corner.

I stepped around the spare speakers and lighting rigs, and there, in the corner by the maintenance channel, I found an electric eel.
Not that I knew much about electric eels, really—I just figured this was the sort of thing you'd call one. Though for all I knew it could've been a swamp eel, or something else entirely.
It lay there plump and round at the edge of a shallow puddle, its tail twisting and slapping the floor. Its eyes were big and bright, a little lost—maybe even a little sorry for itself. Beneath the blue sheen of its skin, tiny arcs of electricity sparked now and then from the tip of its tail.

Zzzt—

It had to be an electric eel.

I crouched down and watched it carefully.
"Inspector, there's a stranded electric eel over here," I said.

"An eel?"
"No, an electric eel."

I found a towel and tried to drape it gently over the eel. It squirmed, but didn't try to get away—just curled its tail up, like a little animal afraid of being scolded.

The moment my fingertips touched it, a faint tingle ran up through my glove.

"It looks like it could really use some help, Inspector."

After Shiro arrived, she ran a quick scan of it. The device flashed red, then spat out a string of data I couldn't make sense of.
It didn't take long, though—or rather, I'd known the answer all along.

It was an Anomaly.

Once the scan was done, the "electric eel" was placed in a containment box backstage for the time being.
When I looked at it, it flicked its tail with a wet splat.

"So... it isn't an electric eel?"
The Inspector didn't seem to pick up on that strange feeling. Then again, even I only had a vague hunch.
Object Anomalies are harder to sense than humanoid ones, after all.

Shiro nodded calmly.
"To be precise, it's a stun gun that's been afflicted into the form of an electric eel."
"It should be security-team gear, but for whatever reason it got left behind back here, and something triggered its Affliction."
Shiro considered it a hazard; by protocol, it had to be held in isolation for further observation.

It wasn't really my place to stop any of it, and besides, her call was the right one.

Squelch.

The strange thing was, it didn't like anyone getting close. If a crew member so much as walked past, the blue arcs across its body would flare up all at once, sending them stumbling back. But whenever I came near, it would settle.
Inside the little square box, it gave a pitiful little wriggle.

I looked at it through the clear wall of the box.

"Did you end up like this because you were afraid?"

It didn't answer, of course.

Amid the hum of the water filter, I couldn't shake the feeling that there was some strange emotion in its eyes.
A longing for freedom? Or for the sea?
But from the moment it became an Anomaly, those longings had already turned into dreams forever out of reach.

A lost child... I thought.
And for some reason, without quite meaning to, I found myself softly humming the melody from the day's performance.

The blue glow at the tip of its tail flickered, and—as if it had finally heard something—it slowly settled down.

It happened at dusk.
Just before the final show was due to start, the Pathos Particle anomaly index began to spike. As layer after layer of dark purple ripples welled up across the performance pool, the backstage alarms blared, shrill and grating.

"Affliction detected in the water circulation system. Anomaly source moving rapidly toward the performance pool."

The crowd was evacuated fast. And right then, still in my stage costume, I found myself on the evacuation list too.
Though, personally, I had no intention of going along with it.

So I thought of the "electric eel."

If it had once been a gun, then surely it hadn't been built to hurt innocent people. It must have had a purpose of its own—someone, something it was meant to protect. It had just forgotten all of that after the Affliction.
But in its eyes, I couldn't find any of that obsessive craving. Only a clear, pure longing for the sea.

I pressed my hand lightly to the wall of the box.
It leaned its head toward me in turn.
Through the clear material, I heard a faint zzzt.

I could hear my own heartbeat—and, farther off, the crew calling my name in alarm.

I opened the containment box and reached out to it.
"You don't exist to hurt anyone, do you?"

The blue current stung my fingertips numb.
The next moment, within a beautiful flare of electric arcs, its fish form peeled away like a bursting bubble, revealing the silver-white body of the gun beneath.

I closed my hand around it.

And then, the blue light fell.

As planned, the show would resume in twenty minutes, so the crew were working flat out on their final checks, leaving no room for error.

The light of dusk fell across the pool.
The water rippled, as though overlaid with a sheet of gold leaf.
Apart from the water that had spilled over into the spectator stands, you'd never have guessed any chaos had happened here at all.

The Inspector found Triss backstage.

"I really should be reprimanding you—for leaving your post without authorization, and for using an unverified Anomaly in combat…"
"But thank goodness you're safe."

Now, though, it no longer looked anything like an electric eel.

"The Affliction hasn't fully faded, but it's dropped to a manageable level. Logistics can carry out a stabilization refit."
Shiro gave her verdict after a brief examination.

"If you insist on putting it that way, then yes—you could see it like that."

"Empathy is one of Triss's strengths as a Combatant—but please keep it balanced. Don't let her become a weakness of yours."

Before long, Triss was issued a new piece of equipment—
a Pathos Weapon, painstakingly refitted by the Logistics Division.

"Little Eel."

Despite having no experience in martial arts or acting...
 
—I must give it my all.
I can't let them down, no matter what.

On the timeless training grounds, a gentle breeze seemed to whisper tales of long-forgotten martial legends.
 
"Hey-ya!"

—Is this good enough?

With filming only three days away, I needed to push myself to the limit to achieve perfection for the promo.
 
As night enveloped the training ground, a lone lamp cast a warm, amber glow.
Thrust the hips, kick the leg!
"Hyaah!"

Clenching my teeth, I repeated to myself—It's fine, I can handle this.

I still felt like a burden to everyone...

"The interplay of Yin and Yang gives rise to all creation—"

A long-buried, indescribable feeling began to resurface—

"Yin and Yang sustain each other—when one reaches its peak, the other rises."
"Excessive self-restraint causes the heart to wither under suppression, while excessive indulgence leads the spirit into recklessness and chaos."

Since arriving on Castaway Island, I had been asking locals about playing the conch, but no one seemed to know how.
With the rise of Pathos Energy technology, many ancient and mystical arts had been lost.
Compared to the traditional pastimes, the younger generations of Castaway Islanders were more drawn to the high-tech gadgets from the city.

"Now that I think about it..."
The girl appeared to have an idea.
"There's an elderly Felinian who lives in the lighthouse at the far end of the island."
"My grandpa mentioned she was the lighthouse keeper and had been there since he was a child."
"Every night at sunset, a beautiful melody would drift from the lighthouse, as if the ocean itself were singing."
"I wonder... could it have been her playing the conch?"
Her story sparked a glimmer of hope in me.
If I could find this lighthouse keeper, perhaps I could learn the ancient skill.
"That's wonderful! Can you tell me how to find her?"
The girl scratched her head, looking a bit embarrassed.
"The lighthouse is at the other end of the island... but I'm not sure how to get there."

It seemed I would need to find another way.

With the butler's assistance, I located a local fisherman who knew the route.
He took me and the Inspector to the lighthouse in a small boat.

The scenery near the lighthouse was a stark contrast to the beach resort.
While the resort was meticulously designed, this area was raw and natural.
I pushed through the dense undergrowth and followed a cobblestone path that led to the lighthouse. It stood at the end of the trail.
It was aged and weathered. The walls, crafted with intricate stonework, showed signs of significant erosion.
A small cabin connected to the base of the lighthouse, likely the lighthouse keeper's residence.

I knocked on the old wooden door.
"Meow!"
...I took that as a sign I was welcome to enter?
"Sorry to intrude."
I pushed the door open and found a ginger cat inside.
"Good day, madame. Are you the lighthouse keeper?"
"Meow..."
The cat lifted its head to glance at us before darting into the back room.
A few moments later, a Felinian woman with long orange hair emerged.
She wore traditional Castaway Island attire and a necklace made of seashells.
"It's been ages since I had a visitor. I almost forgot how to speak."
"Good day. How may I assist you, lovely young ones?"

The lighthouse keeper welcomed us inside with open arms.
Although the facility was outdated, it was remarkably tidy, reflecting the meticulous nature of the Felinian in charge.
The Inspector and I settled down on the floor while the lighthouse keeper served us some tea.
Once we were comfortable, I shared the reason for our visit.

"So, you want to learn how to play the conch..."
"Yes. It seems not many young people like you are left."
"This place used to be a favorite playground for kids..."
She gazed out the window, lost in memories of the past.
After a moment, she turned back to us, a smile lighting up her face.
"You've traveled a long way. I don't want to let you down."
"Few people even care about these ancient instruments anymore."
"Kids today are more fascinated by the latest gadgets from Catto City. Only old souls like us cling to the traditions of Castaway Island."
"When technology wasn't so advanced, we Castaway Islanders relied on one another to live a carefree life."
"The world is better now, but we've forgotten so many of those cherished old ways."

The lighthouse keeper retrieved a large box from a cupboard.
He lifted the lid, revealing a collection of conches in various colors and sizes.
"Choose whichever conch you fancy. These are the prized possessions I've amassed over the years."
"I'm not sure this is fair... Let me buy it from you, okay?"
"It's no big deal—being able to pass this skill on is reward enough for me."
"Thank you..."
Her kindness and sincerity touched me deeply.
"Then... this blue and white one, if you please."

We arrived at the shore beneath the lighthouse.
"I'll show you how it's done."
The lighthouse keeper lifted a gray and white conch to her lips.
As she blew into it, a gentle breeze flowed through, producing a simple yet enchanting melody.
The sea, the sky, and the musician beside us seemed to merge into one, creating a harmonious chord that echoed the essence of nature.
I followed her melody, tapping my fingers to the rhythm. In the distance, whales began to sing, as if answering her call.

"Now it's your turn."
"Just relax and take a deep breath. Remember to connect with the ocean and blow gently into the conch."
Taking her advice, I closed my eyes, trying to absorb everything around me.
The sea breeze brushed against my face, and the waves lapped at my feet.
I could hear the distant calls of the whales, as if they were cheering me on.
When I opened my eyes again, the vast ocean and sky stretched endlessly before me.
I inhaled deeply and finally blew into the conch.
In that moment, it felt as though I could hear the heartbeat of the ocean, and I instinctively played a tune that matched its rhythm.

Before long, the melody faded.
The whales lingered in the water, and the Inspector smiled at me, offering the gentlest praise as always.
The lighthouse keeper approached us, nodding in approval.
"You have a gift. I didn't expect that."
"You flatter me, ma'am. I just gave it my best shot."
"Keep practicing. I'll teach you everything I know."

And so, I spent more time learning from the lighthouse keeper how to play the conch.
We didn't return to our villa at the resort until sunset.

Meanwhile, in the arena for the Platinum Tournament, Triss expertly guided her whale across the finish line, her athleticism mesmerizing the crowd.
As soon as she stepped off the arena, a swarm of fans rushed toward her.
"Miss Triss! How did you tame that whale?"
"Miss Triss! Can you tell us about the conch you played before the race?"
Overwhelmed by questions, Triss maintained her graceful smile, responding patiently.
"I didn't tame it; we are partners—equal and cooperative."
"We work together to complete the race... to earn honor and prizes."
"Afterward, it will return to the ocean."
"And the key to our bond is this..."
She brought out the blue and white conch and raised it to her lips.
A heavenly melody began to play, harmonizing beautifully with the whale's song, captivating everyone present.

"The music is so beautiful... Just like the stories Grandpa used to tell me..."
"Yes... When I was young, my grandma played those same tunes for me."
"She tried to teach me, but I was too naughty to learn..."
"It's never too late to pick it up now. You could be as good as Triss... well, maybe half as good!"
"What?!"

Triss couldn't help but laugh.
Initially, her interest in the instrument was casual, but now she realized she could truly pass on this skill. It was a delightful surprise.
She thought of the lonely lighthouse and all the diverse people she had encountered on her journey. Her eyes sparkled with determination.
If she could help maintain a peaceful and harmonious bond between people and nature, she would dedicate herself to that cause.

"Great Wizard, if you could make my wish come true..."

"I have but a single wish..."

"No matter how many times I have to reincarnate, can I meet that person again...?"

"I hope..."

In the depths of my sleep, a young girl's voice echoes in my ear. Before I can ponder on it, I jolt awake. Tears slip from the corners of my eyes, dampening my pillow. Gently wiping away the residual tear stains, my hand inadvertently brushes against a storybook on my bedside.

It's a tale from my childhood that I never had the chance to finish.

It's a fairy tale about a girl blessed by the gods and an adventurer raised by a great wizard.

In a kingdom forsaken by the gods, people suffer from calamities. However, with the arrival of a wizard, hope is restored. Before long, a mysterious adventurer appears by the wizard's side. The wizard nurtures the adventurer, teaching him swordsmanship and imparting knowledge of magic.

The wizard then reveals that the world's calamities stem from the existence of the dragons, and only the adventurer's sword, named "Courage", can slay them. Thus, the adventurer embarks on a journey to eradicate the malevolent dragons.

Along the way, he encounters a girl with healing abilities. Her power to heal the wounded is a testament to her divine favor. The moment the adventurer meets the girl, he feels an inexplicable sense of familiarity, as if their lives intertwine in a distant past.

"What a beautiful fairy tale..." As my hand gently caresses the cover of the storybook, I find myself inexplicably drawn to the two characters in the story. Perhaps I'm overly sentimental lately...

It just occurs to me that this adventurer bears a striking resemblance to the Inspector... They're both courageous and virtuous...

The adventurer happens to rescue a maiden from a dragon attacking a village. It's the maiden and the adventurer's first encounter.

The maiden informs the adventurer of her ongoing journey, aimed at reducing the suffering of people.

"Are you not aware that evil dragons frequently lay siege to villages across the world?" the adventurer questions.

How can this seemingly fragile maiden withstand not just the onslaught of dragons, but also the ensuing plague and rat infestations?

"Even if I can only save one person a day, it's better than doing nothing at all."

The adventurer is moved by the maiden's words. Up until now, he has been solely focused on slaying the beasts obstructing his path, never giving a second thought to anything else. However, at this moment, a strange emotion arises in his heart. Not knowing where this familiar feeling comes from, the adventurer nevertheless decides to protect the maiden. From then on, the two embark on a long journey together.

They pass through many villages, saving numerous lives. The adventurer drives off the evil dragons attacking the villages, while the maiden heals the injured adventurer and the others. Their deeds earn them the gratitude and goodwill of the people. The adventurer, having grown up alongside the wizard, is unfamiliar with the ways of the world. Yet, after meeting the maiden, he gradually begins to understand her feelings.

"Even if I can only save one person a day, it's better than doing nothing at all... right..." As I turn the pages of the book again, I find myself repeating those words. I understand that sentiment very well. I've always been in search of something I can do... The two in the story must feel the same.

I keep turning the pages of the book, even though I am well aware of what is about to unfold...

Later on, during their journey, the adventurer and the girl encounter companions with minds alike. Not every meeting with these companions is pleasant, yet it's these frictions that solidify the unbreakable bond between them. With the addition of these companions, the adventurer's quest for the dragons hastens. Soon, they find the lair of the dragons.

The adventurer, leading his companions, engages in a fierce battle with the dragons.

However, every story has an ending.
The adventurer ultimately slays the calamitous dragon with his sword. It's then he realizes that although the sword can kill the dragon, the evil power within the dragon is unleashed at the same time. The world is instantly plunged into darkness.

The young boy can't believe what is happening before his eyes. The great wizard who has raised the adventurer told him... No, he has merely instructed him to slay the dragons, claiming they are the root of all evil. He has never mentioned that everything would cease because of this...

At that moment, the great wizard appears before the adventurer. He is just as gentle as the adventurer remembers him to be.

"So it has come to this end after all..." In the end, the wizard reveals the truth to the young boy.

It turns out that the adventurer and the maiden have experienced countless cycles of reincarnation.

No matter how many times the cycle repeats, the world is destined to fall into ruin due to the malevolent dragon. The only way to prevent this destruction is to unleash the maiden's divine power, but it comes at the cost of her life.

In past cycles, the adventurer was unwilling to sacrifice the maiden, leading to the world's demise. 

In an attempt to break this cycle, the wizard seeks out the young adventurer and teaches him everything in hopes of ending the cycle. However, even with the mightiest sword and magic, the adventurer is unable to change the outcome. Once again, he is caught in a dilemma. 

When the life of a loved one and the safety of the world are placed on the same scale, anyone can understand which is more important. Yet, sentiment often runs counter to reason. 

"...Inspector, what would you choose if you were in this situation?" I can't help but get curious when I happen to discuss this story with the Inspector. 

"Hmm... I think I would choose to save the person in front of me instead of the world..."

"...May I ask why, Inspector?" I am curious about what kind of answer the Inspector would give me.

"If saving the world requires the sacrifice of an innocent girl, is such a world really worth saving?" 

"Perhaps it's just another jest of the gods."

"Besides, what if there's a way to save both the girl and the world?" These simple words seem to unravel my doubts.

"Hmm, your thoughts are indeed unique, Inspector."
 
"Hm?"

"Nothing, I was just thinking... If the young man could think like you, their ending might have been different."

As a child, Triss had a storybook that she liked a lot. Every night, just before drifting off to sleep, she would immerse herself in that story. However, her young self would often fall asleep before reaching the end. Despite this, she cherished the storybook immensely.

The young girl in the storybook, much like Triss, is blessed with divine abilities. Her powers can be used to aid many, and she does so willingly.

Triss is enamored with this character in the story because, in the end, the girl understands the adventurer and chooses to fulfill her destiny. She unleashes the divine power hidden within her, and peace is finally restored to the world.

This is the only gift left by the gods, and it is the fate bestowed upon the girl. The people no longer have to suffer, and the young man's mission is finally over. 

However, the girl that the adventurer has always wanted to protect turns into specks of light and vanishes. He holds back his hand that yearns to grasp the scattered light, but he can't stop the tears streaming down his face.

Triss was still a child when she first read this story. She wept throughout the night because of the story, causing her to miss the true ending of the story.

"Brave girl, your sacrifice brought peace to the world. As a reward for your courage, I'll grant you one wish," says the wizard.

"Great Wizard, if you could make my wish come true..."

"I have but a single wish..."

"No matter how many times I have to reincarnate, can I meet that person again...?"

"This time, I hope to stay by his side longer..."

Many, many years later, when everyone has forgotten what the world used to be like, the young man once again meets the girl at a quiet street corner.

This is just an ordinary story, a story with a fairy-tale ending.

As an adult, Triss understands that reality won't be as beautiful as the story. Yet, she still hopes that this ending can one day become reality...

A bead of sweat traces down my skin, falling onto the hem of my skirt, leaving behind a small, damp mark. I wipe the sticky droplets from my cheek with a handkerchief and glance skyward towards the blazing orb suspended above.

It seems this summer's temperatures are a bit more intense than usual.

The finely crafted gown my family had ordered just for me is exquisite, but... the numerous buttons make it hard to breathe. Thankfully, the Inspector has prepared more comfortable attire for me in advance. Time to change, I suppose.

Softly, I undo the buttons that have been restraining my chest, and the heavy lace falls away smoothly. The hot air seizes the opportunity to invade, leaving a faint blush on my fair skin.

"Mmm..." With the constraining clothes finally loosened, I draw a satisfied sigh, picking up another piece of clothing. The maid's dress the Inspector prepared for me is light and comfortable. It starts to glide from the tip of my fingers, gradually, covering my bare skin. Now, I'm dressed as a maid.

"Alright, let's do this!" After silently cheering myself on, I kick off a day's work as a maid.

Once I put on this maid's dress, I become a restaurant maid, serving others. I listen to their worries and heal their wounds. This is also the meaning the "Baker's Cats" bears to this day.

During a brief respite from work, I approach the busy Inspector, carrying a cup of hot coffee.

"You've been working hard, Inspector. Here's some coffee I brewed for you. Enjoy."

"Also... I've acquired a seaside cafe and I'm thinking of checking it out this weekend."

As soon as I finish, everyone stops their tasks at hand, turning their intense gazes towards me. I tugged at the hem of my skirt.

"So... I'd like a day off..."

"I want to go too!" Echo breaks the silence first.

"Together."

Then, it's the Inspector's voice. I lift my head, unprepared, and met the Inspector's eyes, beaming with joy.

"Let's all go together."

"This is the place... Are you certain you wish to purchase it?" 

The weathered key slightly turns in the lock, and the elderly shopkeeper nudges open the restaurant's door.

Contrary to the long-standing symphony of laughter and banter that we're used to, we are greeted by heavy and damp air. Dust blankets the bar; chairs are strewn about in disarray. In this perennially closed seaside dining establishment, the ocean breeze is its only visitor.

I survey the mess before me with a sense of distress. The display bar is missing a corner. The coffee machine's power cord is severed. The sea's salty air has eroded the door... I can tell Echo is trying to say something... After all, no matter how one looks at it, the place is hardly in the condition to sustain a regular operation.

"Shall we consider another place?" Asura kindly suggests.

Suddenly, a gust of sea breeze gently ruffles my hair. I look at where the breeze came from and behold the sight that it has traversed—fluttering curtains, gleaming floor-to-ceiling windows, a delicate beach, tranquil waves. The scent of the sea meanders through the restaurant's windows, wafting in with a languid grace. And then, there's the Inspector... who's standing silently by the window and watching me without a hint of complaint.

"No, let's stick with this place." I tear my gaze away from the Inspector and look at everyone. "Would you all lend me a hand?"

There's much work to be done. To create a comforting environment that can soothe the spirits of our patrons, it's time for me to roll up my sleeves and get to work.

Most patrons at the Baker's Cats are struggling with emotions they can't let out.

Whether it's facing Anomalies on the frontlines or serving customers as a maid, there's only one thing I must do.

"Here's your coffee."

I present the customer at the bar with a "Mood Coffee", designed to soothe one's mood. But as he drinks, his worries are not being alleviated; instead, he begins to sob.

"...Why is life so painful?"

I cannot answer this question. My "dream" is to heal those with troubled hearts and ease their sorrow. However, the "power of comfort" can only provide temporary solace, but cannot truly help them escape their suffering.

The sea breeze against my cheek seems to grow colder. 

Time went by quickly. In a blink of an eye, the sun is already setting.

I walk slowly, cradling a heap of newly arrived items. They pile up like a small hill, obstructing my view, so I fail to notice the Inspector approaching head-on.

Bang!

In the collision, my skirt flies up and countless items scatter through the air. Instinctively, I hold down my skirt, but I'm about to fall to the ground—

"Triss!"

—The Inspector grabs my hand.

"Are you hurt?"

"I'm fine... Thank you, Inspector."

The warmth in my palm and cheeks subtly intensifies. To avoid being noticed, I hurriedly let go of the hand. Thankfully, I think the Inspector saw nothing just now.

After picking up the scattered items and standing up, I survey the restaurant. Although everyone has been helping, the renovation progress is slow. We've yet to purchase new coffee equipment, and the front door remains in disrepair, lying in a heap. Most importantly, not a single customer has come to visit thus far.

Running a seaside restaurant is even more challenging than I imagined.

The ocean's tides lap gently around my ankles, its ebb and flow a soothing rhythm. Far in the distance, where the sea and the sky meet, a pod of whales and the slowly descending sun are both bathed in the soft hues of twilight.

The Inspector and I are walking side by side on the soft, fine sand, leaving footprints behind us. 

"Inspector, is my dream to run a seaside restaurant... misguided?"

"Haha, I think it's a wonderful idea. That way, you can share Mood Coffee with more people."

The Inspector doesn't question my "dream". It's as if... we're always heading in the same direction, walking the same path.

The Inspector's "dream" is to transform the restaurant into a sanctuary for those burdened with worries.

Anyone who came here, after savoring the carefully brewed "Mood Coffee", would find solace for their soul.

However, the souls seeking comfort never cease to arrive. Even after healing all the customers who visited, there are still many people in unreachable corners, waiting for emotional solace.

"Thanks for the coffee! It's just that the place is too far, I have to spend a lot of time getting here..." A departing customer said this during our farewell.
 
After the customer has left, the Inspector sighs and said, "I wish I could open restaurants all over Catto City... maybe one by the sea."

Those words turn into an unforgettable resonance, echoing in the depths of my heart.

"...Achoo."
As the warmth of the evening sea breeze fades, I let out a small sneeze.

Just then, something warm gently falls. "Let's head back, better not catch a cold."

Warmth slowly seeps into my heart.
Looking up, it's the Inspector who has draped a coat over my shoulders.
In the gentle twilight that seems almost molten, the Inspector smiles at me.

"If you are worried about not having enough customers, I have a suggestion."

"...?"

"This is the internet-famous restaurant personally managed by Miss Triss, where it's as challenging to score a seat as it is to find a diamond!"

"Oh! Miss Triss, give me a chance!"

What was once a desolate beachside diner is now crammed full of "tourists" from all over. They push and shove against each other, clawing at the floor-to-ceiling windows. They eagerly stare inside the diner as if their gaze can shatter the windows and allow them to break in—

Swoosh!

—and then they're blocked outside by the curtains.

After several days of intense renovation, the formerly decrepit beachside restaurant is completely transformed. The exterior is bedecked with layers of vibrant decorations, while the interior features pristine, fully stocked coffee utensils.

And...

"Let the summer heartbeat continue to the end of the sea."

Above the entrance, a large electronic screen is embedded, endlessly playing a promotional video featuring Triss. In the video, Triss, dressed as a maid, rides a whale breaking through the waves, firing streams of pink hearts towards the camera.

"...I might have overdone it a bit." Watching herself spread love hearts everywhere on the screen, Triss smiles wryly.

But considering this was the Inspector's suggestion, she can't help but... act unlike herself.

"Triss looks very happy in the ad, it's nice."

The oblivious Inspector nods and turns to ask: "So, Triss, why did you want to start a seaside restaurant?"

How should she answer that?

Triss gazes at the Inspector in front of her. This is someone who has "dreams", always tirelessly working for others. The Inspector must be a source of "healing" to others and to herself. With this thought, she smiles and closes her eyes.

"Because... I want to heal more people."

...But really, it's because of you.

For now, however, let her suppress these complex thoughts deep inside and focus on being a diner maid.

In a bygone year, I stumbled upon a quaint mountain hamlet, where I chanced upon a peculiar individual.
She sat by the roaring flames of a forge, yet not a sweat was seen on her forehead.
Her gaze seemed to penetrate, as if she was looking at something invisible.

I ambled over and greeted her.
"I am in search of the most renowned bladesmith in these parts."
"I know nothing of such a bladesmith. In the nearby villages, I am perhaps the only one who practices the art of forging."
"Then, I seek to commission a blade. What would be the cost?"
"Cost? I require no money. Nevertheless, only the finest of meteoric iron would merit my craftsmanship."
"The finest of meteoric iron?"

Could she be another one of those vainglorious bladesmiths I've previously encountered?
"Scientifically, meteoric iron is merely iron containing trace amounts of other metallic elements..."
"So you don't believe me. Then why bother seeking me?" She sighed heavily.
"Crossing millions of light years, embodying countless yearnings and remembrances..."
"If you fail to comprehend even this, you might as well leave."

I see now.
If one were to convert yearnings and remembrances into the concept of Pathos Particles, I might begin to understand.
It seemed that this bladesmith was indeed a bit extraordinary.

It didn't take me long to learn the whereabouts of the meteorite iron.
In a neighboring abandoned village, there lived a young man who was rumored to possess a piece of meteorite fallen from the sky.

"Word has it you have a meteorite. I'd like to buy it from you—name your price."
I found the young man without much trouble.
At the time, he was sitting at the entrance of the desolate village, gazing blankly at the distant mountains.

"I can give you the meteorite, but I don't want money."
It seemed that money had lost its appeal in this day and age.
"On that mountain, there's an Anomaly. If you can bring it to me, you can take not only the meteorite but also anything you want from this village."
An Anomaly, huh? During my wanderings, I had indeed met quite a few people similar to this young man.

"You should know that although humans can turn into Anomalies, Anomalies cannot revert back to humans."
The young man was taken aback.
"I... see... Then just bring me something from its body."
He spoke these words slowly.

The next day, I came down from the mountain and handed the young man a blood-stained jade half-piece. He took out the other half from his chest, fitting them together to form a complete jade ring. Silently, tears streamed down his face as he threw both the meteorite and the jade ring at me.

"Take them. They're yours now."

The blacksmith glanced at the meteorite iron I presented, her eyes focusing for the first time.
"So soon you've procured meteorite iron? ...Wait, what's this?"
"Can this jade pendant be used as material for forging a blade?" 
She pondered for a moment, then nodded, put away the pendant, and retreated into the room behind her.
"The forging will take some time. Come back in a few days."

I chose not to kill time elsewhere, but sat beside the blacksmith's furnace, waiting. 
That wait stretched into three days.
After three days, she emerged, holding a long sword, and presented it to me.
"Here, take it. Don't bother me again if it's not important."
After a moment, she added,
"And even if it is, don't."

As I drew the sword, the gentle friction of metal sounded as crisp and pleasing as the tearing of silk.
The Pathos Particles within me began to flow unconsciously into the blade's crystal-clear edge, and I felt a wave of heat and cold from the sword.
In a daze, it seemed I saw something.

Underneath the moon, an Afflicted man extended his sharp claws toward a young boy. 
Blood splattered, and the boy realized in shock that it was his mother who had fallen, sacrificing herself to shield him. 
Looking into the boy's burning, rage-filled eyes, the Anomaly seemed to regain a shred of consciousness. It started to hesitate, then turned and fled, never to return.

Now I see. No wonder when I struck, the expression on the Afflicted man's face was not one of pain or wrath, but one of guilt and relief.
I feel like... I could use a drink.

For a long stretch of time that followed, this blade was my closest confidant. 
It was my safeguard, protecting everything I held dear, never once letting me down.
The edge of this sword severed both Anomalies and humans alike, along with countless trivial malevolent thoughts.

Until one day, weary of my nomadic existence, I heard a peculiar rumor.
A rumor is but a rumor—normally, I would have no interest in chasing down so-called truths.
After all, in this chaotic and despairing world, truth is often an extravagant luxury.
If time can be spared, it would be better spent sharing a drink with a friend.

However, this rumor was different. It was tied to certain matters compelling me to venture to a place known as Catto City.
Of course, before doing so, I would need to assume a new identity—and this blade, naturally, could not be openly carried with me any longer.

Unsheathing the sword, I gently drew out the long blade. As my fingers brushed over the blade, its icy touch gave me an illusion of kinship. At some indistinct moment, I began to comprehend the words of the swordsmith. "Stars spanning millions of light years, embodying longing and nostalgia..."
If only such a day would come when I could express my longing and nostalgia directly to others.
With these thoughts, I returned the blade to its scabbard and placed it into a prepared box.

It's that time again, the day set aside for routine maintenance of the weapon.
Opening the long-sealed box, a cloud of dust and a rush of nostalgia fill the air.
A wooden box of maintenance tools is neatly put on the floor. Only then does Minami Yayoi draw the blade from its scabbard. 
Despite not having been used for quite some time, it still gleams like clear water, like a fiery blaze encased in ice.

"...A sword? It's quite beautiful"
The Inspector's familiar voice queries curiously from behind.
"Yes, it was once a star."
"A star? What does that mean? Where did you get it from? Come on, tell me more..."

"Inspector, asking a lady about her past is just as impolite as asking her age, wouldn't you agree?"
"Alright, alright, I won't ask then."
Seeing the Inspector suppress his curiosity brings a sudden lightness to Minami Yayoi's melancholic mood.
"It's not anything special, really... Inspector, would you care for a drink with me?"

"Huh, why the sudden urge for a drink?"
"What are we drinking? I want in too!" Echo bursts into the room, followed by an unamused Asura and an ever-expressionless Shiro.
"Echo forced me to eavesdrop."
"Asura! How could you betray me!"
"Underage drinking is prohibited, so you'll be having juice, Echo."
"Shiro!"

Looking at this group of kids bickering brings a sense of levity that brushes away any lingering gloom. With that thought, Minami Yayoi returns the blade and maintenance tools back into their box.
"Shiro, allow me to treat everyone to drinks today. But remember, it's only for today!"

I'd never planned on entering these so-called races.
A pack of riders, circling a fixed course lap after lap, all to pull ahead of the rest.
Pull ahead—and then what? Gear up for the next round of the same thing?

No prey, no spoils—and yet it's exactly the kind of thing people never tire of.
I didn't see the appeal. But the figure they were offering was genuinely hard to refuse.

"Look at its elegant frame—all custom-built to your specifications, of course."
I glanced at the rep. Sharp suit, not a thread out of place. He was making his pitch, rattling on about the lightweight aluminum-alloy frame, the retuned suspension, the control software reprogrammed for faster cornering, and the Pathos Armament modifications that carried a faint whiff of illegality.
Perhaps he thought I'd grow attached to the machine.

"We only want you at your very best out on the track."
"My best?"
"Victory, of course," he answered with a smile.
"This invitational has drawn a great deal of attention. With your reputation, your image, and a machine this refined—a smooth debut would be enough to make you the talk of the event."

No surprise there.

The bike, though, really was something.

I walked a slow circle around it, fingertips trailing along the edge of the fairing. I had to admit it: a beautiful little beast.

"So—" I said. "You want me to ride it, win, and smile for the cameras?"

The rep's smile faltered for less than half a second.

"Of course—though we'd prefer to call it a win-win."

"We believe only a rider as elegant and accomplished as you could tame Lunar Trace, Ashen Mist."

After that came the rundown—the event, the publicity, the VIP seating, the team's public image.
The rep in the suit had thought of everything. He'd even drawn up a contingency plan for fending off reporters who got too pushy.

"Miss Ashen Mist, is there something about our arrangements that gives you pause?" the operations head asked delicately.
"No. You've been thorough."
His expression eased, visibly.
"It's just that before I decide whether to race, I'd like to meet the other riders."

The room went quiet for a moment.

"If it's intelligence on the competition you're after, we've already assembled full dossiers on every entrant—past results, preferred racing lines, and—"
"I've seen all of that." I cut him off with a smile.
"I want to meet them in person."

"That would take some arranging, I'm afraid. With the new season nearly upon us, even our own riders train on separate schedules—"
"Then take me where they train."

As it turned out, they couldn't refuse me.

I met my "rival" at the track.

"So you're the celebrity wildcard they slotted in at the last minute?"
She didn't pull her punches. Clearly, she didn't see me as anyone worth taking seriously.
Behind me, the rep went stiff.

"Sounds like I'm already quite famous."

"The organizers plastered your posters everywhere. Hard not to know."
She accepted the water bottle her mechanic offered and took a sip.
"Posters won't get you through the corners, though."

An interesting one. Far more interesting, at any rate, than the people trailing behind me.
"A pity. I'd been planning to let them ride the whole race for me."

"Then you're in for a disappointment."

"Not necessarily. I might just ride better than my own posters."
I smiled and held out my hand.
"Minami. Try not to go easy on me."

"Runner-up," I repeated.

"Got passed on the inside on the final lap last year."
The Felinian across from me handed the empty bottle back to one of her crew. She didn't sound the least bit ashamed of it.
"So this year, I'm taking it."

A very practical sort of revenge.

"And you?" she asked. "Here to scout the competition early?"

"No. I only came to see what, exactly, all of you enjoy about this."

She blinked—then laughed, like I'd asked her the strangest thing in the world.
"Enjoy?" She wiped the sweat from her temple with her thumb.
"Yesterday I ran 47 laps on this track. Another 21 this morning. And so far, my best lap is a whole 0.13 seconds faster than yesterday's."

"Doesn't sound like much to celebrate."

"It isn't." She opened another bottle and tipped her head back for a long pull.
"Which is why I've got two more runs this afternoon."

I watched her.

Not far off, an engine's roar swelled closer, then trailed away.
Another bike, black as shadow, shot out of the pit exit, its rider tucked low, and in a blink it was gone, swallowed by the sunlit track.

The Felinian clearly had no intention of wasting much more time on me. She'd already pulled her gloves back on.
Before she left, as though something had just occurred to her, she turned back to me.
"I hear your bike's fast."
"You mean Lunar Trace? I haven't taken it out yet."

"That's its name? Not bad."
"Then you should. A good rider spends time with her machine."
"Don't let it down."

Lunar Trace was harder to win over than I'd imagined.

It didn't dull its edge simply because I'd become its new owner.
If anything, it felt as though it were testing me—measuring whether I had any right to command it, or whether it would throw me hard onto the tarmac for those "peers" of mine to laugh at.

The runner-up was half a bike-length behind me.

The whole thing had started on a whim, one neither the organizers nor my support team had backed.
I understood their worry. It came down to two things: the fear it would look like infighting, and the greater fear that if I lost to one of these riders out on the track, the myth they'd worked so hard to build would shatter.
But I didn't care.
After all, nothing in the contract stopped me from challenging the other riders during free practice.

Round one.
The two bikes shot across the line almost side by side.
The clock, though, didn't hesitate.

The runner-up pulled off her helmet, glanced at the times on the screen, and took the result in stride.
"Two hundredths of a second," she said.
"Close. But... you won."

"A pity," I said, my voice muffled inside the helmet.
"You ride well."

"Well—say what you like, I was runner-up last year." She paused.
"But can you really afford to be this casual, Miss Ashen Mist?"

"Oh?"

"Your presence rattled me at first, I'll admit it."
The seasoned rider smoothed back the sweat-dampened ends of her hair and pulled her helmet on again.
"But there's a limit to how far talent alone will carry you. One more lap, and I'll leave you behind. What do you say?"
"Is that so?" I smiled. "Then let's run another."

She hadn't been bluffing.
Going into the final sequence of corners, she set up for the inside line earlier than she had on the previous lap, keeping my front wheel pinned behind hers.
By the time I caught on, she'd already taken the ideal exit line, half a beat ahead of me. The gap across the back half was never wide, and yet I never once found a chance to get past her.
At the line, she beat me by half a bike-length.

"This one's mine," she said.

Interesting.

It wasn't a gap in skill, I thought. She was a fine rider, but on skill alone, I was every bit her equal.
Something else had given her that conviction. The conviction that let her read me clean through. And it was something I didn't yet have.

"Shame I can't give you another lap, though. I've got a team appearance to get to."

"Well. Now that really is a pity."
I reached out and touched Lunar Trace's frame. It was still warm from the run. It sat there in silence, like a slender red crescent moon that had only just swept across the night sky.
"Then make it up to me. Tell me why you set up for that line back there."

"Back at Turn Three, you were carrying your weight low." She looked at me again, slowly, from head to toe. And then, at last, she smiled.
"Because there's no time to claw back in the second half of the Cowrie Cove circuit. Come out of Three and Four slow, and there's a twelve-degree climb right after. If you don't shut the door on the rider behind you and take the lead there, you spend the rest of the lap stuck behind whoever's in front. So if you want the position before the straight, you have to commit to the line early."
"I see."

I see.

"So—do you understand now why we keep coming back?"

"A little, now," I said.

"Not enough." The veteran shook her head.
"You'll need to understand a great deal more. Only then will you have a chance to meet me in qualifying."
"I'll do my best not to disappoint you."
"That's supposed to be my line."

And then, sooner or later, it would all get painted over with something new.

I've always liked places like that. Not because the art's any good, really—but because it feels free.

Want to leave your mark? Pick up a can. Want to forget something? Pick up a can. One color over another. A little willful, maybe. But honest.

The older kids from the orphanage would paint there too.
Sometimes simple murals, sometimes clumsy, oversized lettering trying to copy someone else's style.
But most people wouldn't give the kids a hard time over it.

I gave the signpost beside me a shake.

DEAD END.

This is a story from a long, long time ago.

Back then, somewhere, there was an orphanage, and little Minami had lived there for as long as she could remember.

Many children lived there.

At first, no one was any different from anyone else. They shared a room, ate together, played together, listened to stories together—and sometimes, in the dead of night, they'd sneak out to the toolshed in the yard to tell ghost stories.
In those days, someone might burst into tears over not getting the best spot, while someone else might hide away a piece of candy they couldn't bear to eat, only to share half of it with her later that night.

Sometimes, little Minami would wonder why everyone else's ears sat on the sides of their heads while hers sat on top—and why she had a long, fluffy tail while nobody else did.

But she didn't mind.
Those days were long, but full of life, too.

Then, in time, the children began to leave, one by one.

Some were taken in by new families. Some grew up and moved far away. And some simply grew weaker and weaker, until one day, without warning, they were gone.
As the friends she'd grown up with left her one after another, the way people looked at her began to change too—from envy, dependence, and fondness into something distant.

All because she was Felinian.

Time was not fair to everyone.
She was still standing in the same place, while the people who'd once been her whole world were taken from her—just like that.
She couldn't catch up to them. She couldn't make them stay. She could only watch as the nameplates at the head of each bed were taken down, one after another, and replaced with new ones.

So she began to write on the walls.

Not pretty pictures. Not some grand wish. Just small, scattered lines—the kind that got her scolded now and then.

But she didn't mind.
Still, she wrote and wrote.

Until, at last, only one line was left—

"Someday, I'll leave this place too." 

Someday, I'll leave this place too.

And when that day really did arrive, perhaps she, too, would come to miss the girl she used to be.

but after exhausting my efforts with no results, I decided to return to the Inspector for further instructions.

Imagine what the beautiful blue ocean would look like through her eyes
