"Science often resembles superstition until proven otherwise. The reason I brought this up is..."
 
I knew where she was headed. She was reflecting on how my body had started moving when that person took over.
But sadly, this was no longer my top priority.
Call it a shattered soul or a temporary consciousness; this body named "Viola" is just an old, broken vessel.
It doesn't care about the possibility of returning; it only wants to charge headlong into the iceberg.
 
...As for what Viola thinks?
That kid... I believe she'll always have my back.
She loves me unconditionally, just as I love her.

"Unicorn, it's time to go—!"
Perched on a suitcase, the girl zipped down the hill, attracting curious glances from everyone nearby.
Her outfit was far too childish for her maturing form, creating a striking contrast that caught others' attention.
 
"That has to be Twelfth Night, the rising star writer, right? Her works are dark and ghostly. I never imagined she'd be so free-spirited in real life."
"Work-life separation—that's how it should be. I can't help but envy her carefree attitude..."
Before long, everyone seemed convinced by their own analyses and turned their attention elsewhere.
 
Later, Viola arrived at Baker's Cafe in the Quince without any trouble.
"Ins... Oh, In-spec-tor..."
Struggling with the pronunciation, the famed writer scratched her head in frustration.
"Did I say that right? If I mispronounce it, the other me might get upset because she cares so much about what others think..."
Memories of her recent adventures replayed vividly in her mind, like scenes from an enchanting fairy tale.
At that time, she had no control over her body and could only recall vague impressions...
"This person is really kind to the other me...so the Inspector can't possibly be bad! That means it'll be okay even if I mess it up!"
 
Finally, Viola approached the door, feeling reassured.
Gently, she leaned forward.

The summers in Egarudo were hot and dry. This land, nestled between Bocanya and Shyriitrik, had witnessed the harshest of wars.
Nothing could grow in the soil tainted by the Cataclysm, now littered with ruins and curses. It was known as "Where All Gods Fell."

Intangible, sinful fire burned from the crevices, spreading across the land and waiting to claim the lives of anyone who dared approach.
People called it the infernal flame, but I... I lived here... I thrived on the flame.

"I'm starving. I want to eat. Devour! Minotara, I am so hungry!"
"I want to consume a hundred people. I want them to suffer. Torture them, the more pain, the better!"

Then Aria appeared, emerging from the shadows. Her face was a blend of fire and boundless agony, a stark contrast to the sister I once knew.
But she was still my sister, the one I cherished most, the only family I had left.

"Demon! She's a demon!"
"Run! She'll devour us all!"

Aria had heard such accusations for so long that she could no longer discern truth from lies.
What she truly craved wasn't blood and flesh, but Pathos.

Fortunately, I understood that...
The fire secretly burning in people's hearts mirrored the abyssal flame, filled with painful, insatiable desires, and reeking of sin.

It was the scent that Aria longed for.

Many years ago, long before Aria was married...
She had long and silky red hair.
Back then, I was innocent, weak, and easily deceived.

I was the King's illegitimate child, born from lust and wrongdoing.
The King had many illegitimate children, but only my mother was a Felinian.
In Taraku, being a Felinian meant being seen as degenerate.

My innate powers were suppressed by anti-Felinian relics. On the surface, I was a princess, but I lived like a servant.

Aria was my sister, the eldest child and the master I served. She was the only one who ever spoke to me.
She often pretended to dislike her food, giving it to me, a frail and hungry child.
But I was always starving and full of questions.

"What was the ceremony at yesterday's banquet? Why were you speaking on behalf of His Majesty?"
I wasn't allowed to call the King "father" or attend the banquet.

"I knew you'd sneak out... You're a princess. There are dangerous people out there. You shouldn't be in that place."

"You're a princess too, but they call you a Saint? What is a Saint?"
"You shouldn't talk with your mouth full, Minotara. It's rude. Besides, you might choke."

"Then I won't help you with the mutton... or the fish."
"...I will tell you for bedtime stories."

As the eldest princess of the Taraku Kingdom, Aria was destined to marry God.

"The Saint is the princess chosen to wed God. In return, God will bless Taraku with peace and prosperity, empowering the King to conquer his enemies and protect our homeland."
"But the book brought by the last caravan states that we have a typical Everbright Sea climate. There are no natural disasters at all. What help can God provide?"

"Don't be naive. The books may be accurate, but the real world doesn't always align with them. When we face challenges, we all need a bit of extra courage."
"So, are you admitting that God doesn't exist?"

"That's not quite right. If the people believe in God, then God lives in their hearts."
"You don't need to worry too much, Minotara. I'll do my best to preserve what we have for as long as possible, so everyone can live peacefully."

"There's another option! The secret about me..."
In truth, I had already lifted the seal on the relic. If Aria agreed, I could take her away at any moment.

"No, Minotara. Keep your secret to yourself. As for me, since I enjoy the privileges of a princess, I will dedicate myself to the kingdom."
In my memories, Aria was always smiling—calm and cheerful, embracing whatever fate threw her way.

"Minotara, I will pray to God for your everlasting freedom and happiness!"

After Aria married God, the way people treated me improved.
I felt more like a real princess.

"Minotara, God has forgiven your sins. From this day forward, you may call me 'father.'"
"Yes, father."

I mimicked Aria's tone, but deep down, I was anxious.
If it weren't for my sister, I would have already left this place.

But did God truly exist? Had they answered Aria's prayers?
The God I could never reach had shown me no kindness. Only Aria prayed for my well-being.
Perhaps only the Saint, the princess married to God, was allowed to make wishes.

Maybe I should visit her. But I had no idea where God resided.
I sneaked into the King's study, eavesdropping on his conversation with the ministers.

"Your Majesty, God isn't cooperating with our plans…"
"Send more offerings!"
"Ordinary sacrifices aren't enough anymore. God hides away all day, showing no fighting spirit."
"What God seeks is power. Aria is too weak. This is her fault."
"What a useless child... I had such high hopes for her! Archpriest, what do you suggest we do?"
"I believe God is dissatisfied with their wife. It's time we offer a new Saint."

Two thousand nautical miles south of Catto City, across the Ocean of Puzzles, lay the cradle of the Ancient Bauss civilization: the Everbright Sea.

But from his own daughter, the "Betrayer Saint," Minotara.

More specifically, Minotara allied herself with God, betraying the very homeland that had nurtured her.

The scent of blood mixed with sweetness grew heavier,
as if something were pushing the air outward, racing toward the entrance.

"My almighty lord, we humbly summon you to offer a new wife."

"Sister. You should have left this place with me."
"It's not too late. What do other people's expectations matter to us? Sinister, greedy desires will only lead to destruction."
"What we can do for this land and its people is to end it all!"

It all began when the "White Phantoms" emerged.

Even my closest friend wasn't spared.
Her life was cut short by their merciless blades, leaving an unhealable scar in my heart.
 
The Elder explained that these were undead spirits, caught between life and death, driven solely by vengeance.
These aimless ghosts appeared relentlessly. No matter how fiercely I fought, they never seemed to end.
I couldn't comprehend it. Why were these revenants so fixated on my flesh and fur?
If they had once been human, why did they wield their deadly blades against others who shared the same origins?
At that time, I had no answers; all I felt was confusion and frustration directed at a heartless world that revolved only around itself.
 
As night fell and silence enveloped everything, those dark memories surged back, drowning me.
The faces of the phantoms twisted and warped in my mind...
They grinned at me grotesquely, like malignant demons escaped from the inferno, searching for their "Caracal."
To flush my people out of their hiding places, they would go to extreme lengths, setting fire to the entire wasteland. The flames roared, illuminating desperate faces.
 
Even now, the flames that consumed everything still roar in my heart.
I can never forget their heart-wrenching screams...
Or the cherished days that remain vivid in my memory...
Or the promise we made to each other.
She assured me she was only moving to the temple and that she would never leave me.
So...

"...So?"
The dim light in the cold cell felt oppressive.
The face I thought I'd never see again appeared before me.
How long had it been since someone looked at me with care and concern?
It...didn't feel bad.
 
"Loco... Are you alright?"
"What brings you here, Inspector?"
"Oh, I thought I'd check on you. I noticed you were having a bad dream, so I woke you up."
 
"Bad dream? Ha, you could say that. I was just napping, and old memories came flooding back."
"Maybe I've been living too comfortably here, and it's made me complacent."
I turned my face away, glancing at the Inspector from the corner of my eye.
See? The moment I showed even a hint of vulnerability, this person became genuinely concerned.
Unlike those who regarded me with disdain and fear, I could only see pity and sympathy in this human's eyes.
That alone was enough to pique my curiosity.
 
"Were you dreaming about the past?"
These gentle words revealed the Inspector's care for me.
My heart was torn between caution and affection, just as my body itched to be free from these bindings.
 
"Would you say something to comfort me if I said yes?"
"Of course. We're friends..."
Whenever I tried to get closer, this person would instinctively pull away. Was keeping distance their way of showing tenderness?
"But today, I have something different to share."

"But today, I have something different to share."
The sudden pause hinted at hesitation and deep thought.
"You see... Even though Fata's trick has contained your power, your mere presence still attracts a lot of attention."
 
"I understand. To everyone else, I'm still a murderer with crimes that can never be forgiven. It's better for me to stay locked up."
 
"...The council has thought about that, but that's not why I'm here."
The person spoke with serious sincerity.
"To ensure you're properly supervised, I will be your caretaker from now on."
"That works for me. I'd rather be cooped up with you than stuck in this prison."
"I won't confine you, and you won't have to remain in jail. We've arranged with the authorities for you to stay at Whispering Teahouse, under the watch of Fata and Qi."
"I thought you were going to be my caretaker?"
 
"Exactly. I'll vouch for you as long as you don't harm anyone, and I won't interfere with your daily life."
"In other words, you can live there like an ordinary Felinian."
 
Ordinary Felinian?
What does "ordinary" even mean?
I didn't voice that question.
I knew what answer this person expected when they mentioned living like an "ordinary" Felinian.
 
"Don't worry. Everyone here will support you."
Maybe because I hadn't responded, they added,
 
"It seems both Felinians and humans want to extract value from you, exploiting you..."
"Rest assured, we'll handle that. We won't let anyone manipulate you like a pawn."
I remembered the promise they had made.
 
"Okay. Thank you."
I hadn't expressed gratitude in a long time, so these words felt almost foreign.
Perhaps from the moment we first met, I had begun to feel drawn to this person.

After that, I arrived at Whispering Teahouse.
Since then, I've never seen that person again.
Sometimes, I find myself wondering if they are still keeping tabs on me.
 
"What's on your mind? If something's bothering you, why not tell me about it?"
I hadn't noticed when Qi appeared behind me. She sat down beside me, her warm smile brightening the moment.
"..."
"Ah, you seem lost in thought... Do you miss someone?"

She was the playful type, way too familiar with the jungle beyond the base walls—the so-called Forbidden Zone.
And me? I'd been stuck inside for years. But I'd pieced together plenty on my own.
A mental map was forming.

But escaping? I couldn't do that alone.
I needed her. Her strength. Her naivety. Hell, even her trust.

But would she help me?
Help someone as unsavory as her "new friend"?

"Zoe, get over here!"
A hushed call came from the neighboring room, rousing me from my late-night doze.
I rubbed the sleep from my eyes, trying to ignore the ache and fatigue flooding my freshly awakened mind.

Ugh, being pestered by her was nothing new.
By now, her noise was background static. I didn't even bother being annoyed.

I walked over and strained up on my tiptoes, peeking through the little window at the young girl.
Cold glass met my fingertips—and with it, a flood of data:
Quartz sand. Limestone.

"Crackle—!"

A sound cut through the noise in my head.

Light erupted from her fingers. Tiny, but blindingly bright.
For a second, that orange-yellow glow warmed the sterile hallway.
I locked eyes with the grinning girl across from me.

"Haha! I was messing around with this when I couldn't sleep, isn't it cool?"
"...Yeah. Cool."

"Ooh, I wanna give it a name! Hey Zoe, you read a lot—what do you think we should call it? Mini-spark?"
"Fireworks." I responded, almost without thinking.

"Huh? Like... actual fire?"
"It's something that releases colorful lights when different metal compounds burn..."
"Ooooh! That's exactly what I did!"

Like a kid with a new toy, Garfire eagerly conjured more "fireworks" in her room.
Light danced on her fingertips—restless as she was.

But "fireworks" shouldn't be this fleeting, this constrained in a dark, cramped space.

The glow lingered in my vision, and suddenly my throat felt tight. A beat passed before the words escaped me.
"...Don't you ever want to leave? To see what's really out there?"

Deep within the base lay a place shrouded in secrecy, accessible only to a select few.
Whenever newcomers arrived, those with the highest clearance always made their way there.
This was where "Talent" was born—that power they called "Wisdom." It was forced into us through herbal infusions, coursing through our veins like a poisoned blessing.
I knew this place held the base's most crucial secrets.
I'd heard it referred to as the "Divine Tree."

To escape the Forbidden Zone, we just needed to create a little chaos and distraction over there.

"Zoe, I tried that method you told me about last time, and I can really control the explosion range now!"
"I've been secretly practicing the explosion formulas you taught me during training. I've got it down cold!"

"...Good, but don't get cocky. We'll need a bit more prep time."
"Ugh...! I wanna go play outside already..."

I'd rehearsed the plan a hundred times in my head—every step, every detail, perfectly calculated.
The blast radius, the timing, the location, the escape route, the rally point—even how long it'd take the guards to react. All accounted for.
I was sure we'd make it out. Together.
Or at least, that's how it was supposed to go.

Then the first explosion hit. And everything went to hell.

It wasn't just inside the base. The rumbling booms echoed outward, shaking the ground all the way to the Forbidden Zone and beyond.
Pathos Energy erupted like a tidal wave. Affliction spread faster than we could run.
The base descended into instant chaos, alarms screaming.

This wasn't Garfire's doing. This was something bigger.
We were finished. All of it—gone.

No time to search for proof!
My fingers snatched random documents, their rough texture registering briefly—material details flashing through my mind before I forced myself to ignore them.
The archive door crashed shut behind me as I fled, abandoning our planned exit through the side courtyard, instead running toward Garfire's detonation point.

The base had transformed into pure chaos.
Humans and Felinians—all equal now in their madness.
This was the Affliction the records warned about.

My unenhanced body moved on pure instinct, dodging attacks with clumsy desperation.

When I reached Garfire's position, there was nothing. Just an empty space where she should have been.
The rendezvous point was just as vacant. No trace. No sign.

This... wasn't part of the plan.

How did everything explode at once?
Where did we miscalculate?

My mind went blank, all coherent thought vanishing except for one name pulsing through my skull...
"Garfire..."

Was she... gone?

The realization hit like a rusty blade twisting in my chest.
I stood frozen, fists clenched so tight my nails drew blood.

We planned everything perfectly. Every contingency. Every variable.
So what did I miss? Or... had I been fooling myself all along?

The stench of burning flesh clogged my throat.

Looking down at my shaking hands, the truth hit me:
The one person who chose to stand with me... would never answer my call again.

"Zoe... Zoe!"
"Wake up!"

"—!"

Zoe's eyes snapped open to find Claire's face hovering just inches from her own—
Claire was leaning over her, brows furrowed in concern.

"What... where...?"
Zoe's gaze was still a bit hazy as she instinctively scanned the room.
The clock on the wall pointed to 3 PM, the desk cluttered with papers and empty coffee cups, the trash overflowing with chocolate wrappers, and a sickly potted plant on the windowsill... Right, this was the Leopard Daily office.
Reality came crashing back. The lingering scent of gunpowder from her dream dissolved into stale office air.

"Were you having a nightmare?" Claire moved a bit closer. "You kept muttering about getting revenge and looking for someone."

"...Yeah, revenge on the one making me work all these overtime hours."
"Pfft! Too bad Iron Rooster's out today. You could've given him hell."

Claire's eyes suddenly lit up with that familiar scheming glint.
"Nightmares mean you're stressed. Let's blow off some steam tonight. My treat!"
"I heard about this wild new place—Elis Bar on Castaway Island. Word is their drinks are absolute garbage... but the place is packed every single night."
"Something's fishy there. I can smell a story brewing!"

"Elis...Bar..."
The name...it matched exactly with the Elis Guild back in Mannava...
Was there a connection?

My head suddenly felt like it was stuffed with wet sand, thoughts turning sluggish again.
Zoe slumped back in her chair like a punctured inflatable toy, all energy draining away.
Her eyelids grew heavy, words slurring together.
"Too...sleepy...You go...without me..."

"You got it! I'll give you the full report later!"
"Get some rest. Honestly, you've been running on less sleep than a night shift guard..."

The words dissolved into the air as consciousness slipped away again.
That familiar darkness embraced me, warm and heavy.

Would she appear this time?

I was born on the Double Ninth Festival, and on the day I joined the Divine Guards, General Rosalyn gave me the name Savanna.
She explained that this festival is a time to honor our ancestors and the elderly. People climb to great heights and wear dogwood to bid farewell to the lush days of summer.
 
From this day forward, plants would say goodbye to their vibrant green, and the earth would transition from green to yellow, signaling the arrival of the harvest.
 
This name represented my farewell to youthful naivety, my journey into a broader world, and my quest for greater heights.
It also signified a bright and promising path ahead.
 
General Rosalyn had much to say that day, but what I remember most is her taking me out for my first meal as a member of the Divine Guards.
One dish in particular stood out—caramelized sweet potatoes, rich and flavorful, unlike anything I had ever tasted before.
 
The chef mentioned that this dish was meant to be enjoyed fresh and wasn't suitable for takeout.
 
What a pity, really—otherwise, I would have brought some back for Jul to try.
Sweet treats like that were her favorites.
 
When it comes to names—be it Jul, Sept, Savanna, or whatever—they all blend together once you get used to them.
 
Honestly, the names of the dishes mattered far more.
Each dish came with its own unique ingredients, preparation methods, and flavors.
 
Sometimes, the name had little to do with the actual food, which made it all the more intriguing.
 
"Buffalo Wings have nothing to do with buffaloes, and Monkey Bread contains no monkeys."
"And Sweetbread isn't bread and doesn't taste sweet at all."
 
During my breaks, I would return to the snowy mountain cave I had called home for years and share stories with Jul about all the dishes I had tried.

Jul didn't have a name at first because, as a child, I was called Sept.
At that time, it was July, and she decided to name herself Jul, implying that she should be the older sister between us.
 
That year, when I was abandoned in the mountains, I was just two months shy of turning five, beginning to form memories.
 
They probably thought I wouldn't survive the snow-covered mountains, so they spoke freely around me, not caring about their words.
After a trafficker sold me to a family, they soon had a child of their own, and I became the unwanted extra.
 
"Offer her to the Lord Mountain Spirit."
Even the year-round snow on the mountain felt warmer than the coldness of human hearts.
 
If Jul hadn't saved me, I might have perished during that unseasonably cold summer.
 
On the surface, Jul appeared gentle and soft, like a cute doll, but in reality, she was as fierce as a bear.
From what I later learned in Catto City, she was likely an Animal Darkrift—an elite among the Afflicted creatures.
 
For Animal Darkrifts, age is measured from the moment their intelligence awakens.
This means Jul was only four years old, even younger than I was.

Jul's cooking was truly terrible.
So, I had no choice but to teach myself. I started by preparing the prey she brought back, and over time, my skills improved.
 
I experimented with every ingredient I could find in the snowy mountains, enduring food poisoning a few times and barely making it through.
But in the end, I became quite a decent cook.
 
I could confidently say my cooking was the best on this mountain.
—Ahem, though I was the only living person here.
 
But hey, first place is still first, even if there's no competition!
Isn't that why they say your toughest rival is yourself? I was the kind of person who constantly challenged myself—a true powerhouse!
 
I was only eight when someone from Cloud City, out gathering herbs, stumbled upon Jul and me.
 
"Hey, young'un—"
Only later did I learn that was how people in Cloud City referred to children.
 
"What are you doing out here in these frigid mountains? You'll freeze into ice popsicles!"
"No mom and dad? You poor thing..."
"Why not come down with me? The Lord Mayor's Office has a place for orphans."
"Life in the town is much better than here in the mountains. Besides, you need to grow and learn to read and write to become a better person, right? That's impossible up here!"
 
Although the lady suggested Jul could come to the town too, she was used to mountain life and didn't want to leave.
 
"Sept, you should go. You're a Felinian, and you can meet more of your kind in the town."
"I'm not going! Why don't you come with me?"
"I have to stay here and take care of our HOME. There's all sorts of delicious food in the town. Go learn a few recipes, and then you can cook for me when you get back!"

Just like that, I was gently coaxed down the mountain.
Perhaps, deep down, I wanted to leave, and Jul must have sensed it, which is why she said those things.
She was intended to offer me an easy way out.
 
The good news was that, as a Felinian, I was born with the innate talent of a Spirit Guide and possessed an excellent physique.
I didn't stay at the orphanage for long before both the Divine Guards and the Spirit Guide Order came calling.
 
General Rosalyn, aware of my friendship with someone from the Darkrift, subtly hinted that joining the Spirit Guide Order might involve researching the Darkrift.
Those reckless, self-indulgent types were nothing like Jul.
Yet the thought of studying my friend's kind always felt strange to me.
 
In the end, I chose to join the Divine Guards.
Defending our home and our people felt like the right path.
 
With hard work and focused practice, I gradually honed both my appetite and my martial skills.
There was something deeply satisfying about making a little progress every day. That's why, after joining the Divine Guards, I pushed myself—both in training and at the dining table.
 
My growth spurt came quickly—I became stronger, ate more, and soon found myself taller than Jul.
 
The Afflicted allowed into the city, much like Jul, managed to control themselves.
Yet, every now and then, their peculiar natures led to hilarious and awkward mishaps.
 
Sometimes, a few would spiral out of control, transforming into vicious anomalies, like monsters from nightmares.
 
More often than not, they reminded me of Jul.
 
If I had brought Jul into the city sooner, perhaps everything would have been different.
She wouldn't have been harmed by rampaging Anomalies, nor would she have hurt herself out of fear of becoming a monster.
Jul would rather die than let darkness consume her and harm others.
 
I lost my family and my home deep in the snowy mountains.
 
General Rosalyn was right.
"Good and evil lie in choice, not in who you are."
Work hard to grow and become stronger. That's the only way to protect what matters to you."
 
I resolved to get stronger.

In the end, Jul was laid to rest in the Cloud City Graveyard as one of its citizens.
Savanna often visited her grave on her days off, bringing fine wine and food.
 
Though it was meant to honor Jul, Savanna ended up consuming all the offerings herself.
 
"I've been coaxed again!"
"I'm not a Captain in the Divine Guards anymore; I'm some kind of envoy now, and I have to travel everywhere!"
 
"By the way, earlier this year, I met a StormEye Chief from Catto City.
"Can you believe it? A Chief—on par with General Rosalyn."
"This Chief isn't just exceptional at their job; they're also an incredible cook with amazing culinary skills."
 
"Didn't you say you wanted to open your own place? Well, that Chief did just that. It's called Baker's Cafe."
"This isn't just a hobby—the Pathos food they serve helps people stabilize their Pathos."
"I tried it myself, and it even works for Anomalies! If this food goes mainstream, staying sane will be so much easier for everyone!"
 
"Thanks to the Chief's help, I discovered that the one who hurt you wasn't acting alone—there's a larger force at play..."
"The Shadow—I'll be tracking down those bad guys from now on."
 
"After I leave today, it might be a long time before I return."
"But don't worry—when I'm back, I'll bring good wine and delicious food to share while I tell you all the amazing stories from my travels."
 
A gentle breeze swept through, rustling the leaves as it danced over the quiet gravestones lining the hillside.
Savanna finished the last sip of wine and stood up.
 
Visitors came to pay their respects one after another, each tombstone heavy with longing.
 
"Time for me to go! I'll do my best to take care of myself, so don't worry!"
 
She was leaving behind her youthful past, setting out to explore new horizons and reach greater heights.
 
"What, just watching from a distance? Why not go over and say a proper goodbye?"
Teased the Lord Mayor from beneath the nearby trees, playfully nudging General Rosalyn.
 
"Why the fuss? It's not like she'll be gone forever."
"Besides, we're all working to protect the same world—what does it matter where we are?"
 
"Tsk, wasn't it you who couldn't sleep at night and came to me to discuss supply arrangements for her?"
"Look at those dark circles under your eyes! There's no way they're from just one sleepless night. With your student leaving on a long journey, I bet you've been tossing and turning for days!"
 
"That's because your Lord Mayor's Office has dumped so much work on me! It's all just work!"
 
From afar, Savanna turned around, bowed, and strolled off with flair.
 
"Hey! Your student never fails to impress me—always so perceptive! She noticed us long ago!"
"Heh, no surprise—it's my student, after all. Mark my words: next time she's back, she might very well take my place."
"But if she wants to pursue something else, I'll support her all the way as her mentor."
 
Love and longing stretched across endless miles, offering unwavering support and courage to those far from home.

The warm afternoon sun bathed the classroom in a soft, hazy glow, wrapping it in a comforting embrace.
As the teacher droned on from the podium, my mind began to drift, wandering far from the lecture.

"The essence of cultivation lies within your heart."
After we learned the family's Mantra, our teacher delivered daily lectures on those elusive concepts of cultivation.
She urged us to quiet our minds and look inward.
To ponder, understand, and truly internalize the essence of the Mantra.
According to her, meditation was the simplest path to enlightenment.

Yet the idea of "enlightenment" is quite fascinating; For some, it struck like a bolt of lightning, while for others, confusion lingered indefinitely.
I wasn't convinced the teacher was entirely correct; meditation had never really clicked for me.
My first genuine insight into the Mantra came from an unexpected moment: While desperately trying to save a drowning child, a surge of clear water wrapped around my hand, transforming into a long arm that pulled the child to safety.

I watched in awe as the Mantra shimmered to life on my palm. I clenched and released my fist, feeling droplets of water form in my hand.
A wave of pride surged within me, banishing all traces of drowsiness.

"Hey! Big Sis Tara! Are you up for an outing later?"
A friend behind me poked my shoulder, snapping me back to reality.

"Absolutely! I'm planning to try a spicy method of cultivation. Do you think 100 times the spiciness could unlock my true potential?"
We began plotting our next adventure in the corner of the classroom.

That was how I approached cultivation back then, believing that "following my heart" was the key to my journey.

"Gurgle—"
Cold water jolted me awake, but my body kept sinking, my mind slipping away.
Darkness enveloped me... Cold seeped deep into my bones...
Until a hand grasped me tightly.

My memory faded there, and as raindrops brushed against my face, I returned to the present.
Now dressed in mourning black, I stood in a quiet, empty courtyard.
Looking up, I saw their smiling faces framed in black and white...
A wave of cold memories washed over me:

Our car had been swept into the lake by a sudden flood, with my friends—my adventure crew—still trapped inside.
I had channeled the Mantra to shield myself and a few others, getting them safely to shore...
In desperation, I plunged back into the lake to search for the rest...
I found them... But no matter how hard I tried to summon the Mantra, it wouldn't respond...
Until everything faded to black...

A sharp pang of sorrow pierced my chest, stinging my eyes. I turned and ran, racing down the rain-soaked road.
"Why? WHY?!
"Why couldn't I save them?!"
"Why didn't the Mantra work?!"
I shouted, trying to release my frustration and guilt.

The cool rain cleared my mind momentarily, but regret soon took its place. I walked with my head hung low, drifting aimlessly.

"Tara, come on in."
I froze for a moment. Then raised my head to find myself standing at the teacher's door.
"Teacher, why didn't my Mantra work..." I asked, my voice hollow.

"Your cultivation... isn't strong enough yet..."
That was the only thing I could recall from my teacher's words that day.

The mountain road was awash with rain, and the ominous rumble of rocks and mud echoed down from above the village.
I pressed my palm against the damp rock wall, channeling the floodwaters toward the lake using the Mantra.
"I can do this! I won't fail this time!"

"Tara! Wake up! We're almost home!"
The phantom call sent a chill down my spine.
The rain seemed to freeze mid-air, transforming the sky into a vast, dark lake.
I found myself standing at the lake's bottom, gazing up at a distant light that felt forever out of reach.

Memories I had tried to bury surfaced with startling clarity:
At the dark, icy lakebed, I swam desperately toward a slowly descending figure.
I grasped her wrist and invoked the Mantra, creating bubbles that enveloped us all as I swam with every ounce of strength toward the surface.

But the power of my Mantra was fading rapidly, and my awareness began to blur.
Gurgle—
The salty, bitter water filled my throat, and my legs felt as heavy as lead.
Suffocation, dizziness, and the crushing weight of darkness closed in around me.

"Am I going to die...?"
Just as that thought crossed my mind, I felt a gentle tug on my hand.
I forced my eyes open and saw her smiling as she released my grip.
Her lips moved, silently uttering something, and then, with her last ounce of strength, she pushed me toward the surface.

At the village entrance, the mudslide split in an unusual manner, diverting toward the lake as if it had encountered an invisible barrier.
The rain began to ease, and the roaring flood gradually subsided, prompting cheers of relief from the villagers.

I stood at the village entrance, staring up at the gray, overcast sky as fragmented memories clicked into place like pieces of a puzzle.
This time, I finally recalled the words spoken at the bottom of the lake—
"Just... survive."

"Tara, what are your plans after graduation? Will you stay with your family, or venture out into the wider world to cultivate?"
"Staying home means I might have to take over the family business, and honestly, that sounds like a real headache... I'd much rather carve my own path in cultivation."
"Geez... That kind of ambition is sure to stir up some envy, you know?"
"Hee-hee!"

"Tara, come over here."
My teacher appeared at the classroom door, looking noticeably slimmer than before.

"So, you've made up your mind about your cultivation journey?"
"Yeah, I've made my choice."
"Most cultivators train and meditate where their families direct them, but you want to forge your own path."
"You know me, teacher—I think best when I'm on the move. I'd go stir-crazy just sitting around meditating all day."
"No cultivator I know runs around like you do. It's more like a holiday than training!"
She shook her head, her tone a mix of reproach and concern, but her eyes revealed her reluctance to let me go.

"How's your cultivation coming along?"
"Seriously? You're asking the cultivator who stopped a whole mountain flood? I'm pretty strong, you know."
"I meant, how are you doing on the inside?"
She placed a hand over her heart, her gaze deep and gentle.

"What happened that day... will haunt me for the rest of my life..."
"But I've come to realize they never blamed me for it."

Pleased with my response, my teacher nodded.
"Tara, congratulations—you've graduated now.
Keep pushing forward on your journey."
As I watched her leave, a whirlwind of emotions surged within me.

The journey of cultivation continued.
This time, I carried their hopes and dreams with me as I stepped into the unknown.

April returned, and a gentle drizzle fell onto the lake, creating tiny ripples.
Someone stood alone by the water, holding an umbrella and gazing into the distance.

"Remember when I was a kid, calling myself the 'Big Sis'?"
"Back then, I was the only one who mastered the Mantra, always showing off to you."

A soft breeze swept by, and the trees by the lake swayed as if they understood her words.

She chuckled, a hint of pride in her voice:
"Now I can manipulate water with so much finesse, and I even saved an entire village with my abilities!"
"That's quite an achievement, isn't it?"

The rustling leaves grew louder, echoing the applause of excited children.

She extended her hand into the rain, relishing the refreshing coolness.
"You know, if the roles had been reversed back then—if you all had the talent and I was the one who sank to the bottom of the lake..."

A leaf floated down onto her hand, and the breeze calmed.

For a moment, she froze, then let out a bittersweet smile.
"Yeah... if I were in your place back then, I'd have let go too and pushed you all up..."

Tara clasped her hands together and bowed toward the lake.
"I promise—I'll live well, carrying your blessings in my heart."

With that, Tara turned and walked away, Catto City awaiting her in the distance.

What is life like when luck is always on your side?
 
A serious illness once spared me from my family's harsh trial. One rainy day, I forgot my umbrella and unexpectedly ran into a friend just as they were about to head out under the eaves. Even when I've gotten lost, I've stumbled upon breathtaking landscapes.
 
It felt like a gentle stream, free of dangerous rapids or disturbances.
 
I was truly grateful for a life like this.
Yet, every now and then, an inexplicable sadness would creep in.
 
"Fon is so lucky! With just a little preparation, she aced the trial. She hasn't fully mastered the Mantra yet, but I bet she's close—don't you think?"
"With her luck, it wouldn't surprise me if she became the youngest in our clan to master the Mantra. The elders are watching her closely."
"Haha, I'm seriously jealous. If only my life could be as smooth as hers..."
 
Is a smooth life merely the result of wishful thinking?
All those hours of hard-earned sweat during training, the exhausted gaze from sleepless nights... Were those part of fate's blessing?
Was it all just luck, or was it proof of my own efforts?
Couldn't they see?
 
Born into a family that revered luck, I never doubted its existence.
While luck may have paved my path, every step I took was my own.
 
I took a deep breath and lifted my gaze to the sky.
Under the brilliant, almost ethereal sunlight, my damp heart warmed and dried, and I smiled once more.
 
"It's okay. It's fine," I reassured myself.
"Next time, I'll show them what I'm truly capable of."

"Fon was born during a sunshower. She's definitely blessed by fortune!"
My parents' proud voices echoed with firm belief and heartfelt wishes.
Naturally, I chose to pursue the power of rain among all the Mantras.

Every day, I trained diligently, aiming for the heights expected of a "lucky one."
Yet, contrary to everyone's expectations, I didn't quickly master the Mantra nor awaken the mark branded on my waist since my day of choice.
Those who initially watched with amusement grew uneasy. The slow response of my Mantra quietly challenged the deep-seated belief in our clan that luck naturally bestowed mastery over Mantras.
If luck's blessing fails, what happens to our faith?

In that stifling atmosphere, attention gradually shifted away from what truly mattered.
As a child supposedly favored by the Goddess of Luck, I was locked away, required to connect with the divine.
My power, left idle for too long, grew sluggish, like raindrops trapped in clouds, unable to break free.

What was this so-called "power of luck," after all? It was faith, but merely a footnote in true cultivation.
The true focus should be on cultivation itself; anything else was a distraction.
Yet now, they were telling me to gain power through prayer...
Defiance and doubt began to sprout.

Finally, I managed to escape and sat by the cliff to catch my breath. The wind howled past my ears, cool and filled with the taste of freedom.
For the first time, I considered challenging the Goddess of Luck—a bold and reckless idea.

If I were truly blessed by luck, surely I could jump from here and walk away unscathed, right?

I wasn't certain if I was genuinely challenging fate or simply releasing my pent-up feelings.
I spread my arms wide as the gusting wind billowed my sleeves and hem—like golden wings granted by nature.
And then, I leaped.

"Listen, kid, if you're feeling stressed, just talk to us. Don't do anything like this again..."
"Mom, Dad, I promise I wasn't trying to commit suicide! I was just... testing an idea!" I pleaded, but they interrupted me.
"Alright, alright, no need to explain further. We'll handle the clan elders. They were really shaken up, so I doubt they'll bother you again."
"No, you don't understand, I wasn't—"
"Just take it easy for now! If you're uncomfortable in the hospital, let us know."
"Mom, Dad—"
Before I could finish, my parents hurried out of the room, likely to speak with the clan elders.

What was meant to be a daring experiment had turned into a complete disaster, all because of my, well... hasty execution. Everyone assumed I was trying to end my life. No matter how many times I insisted I had backup plans, they just wouldn't believe me. After all, there was that little incident... like, say, a broken leg. So here I was, stuck in the hospital.

"Sigh..."
At least after all that commotion, the clan finally eased up on me. I finally had the chance to explore a different path—the one the elders avoided because it made them uneasy—delving into the power of Rain. However, our lands were so lush and vibrant that I could never use my rain-making abilities freely without disrupting the delicate ecosystem.
So, I came up with another bold idea.

Sure, my last bold idea didn't go so well, but that wasn't going to stop me now.

After a tremendous amount of effort—and I mean a lot—I finally convinced my parents and the clan elders that I wouldn't act recklessly, and I made my way to the Scorching Sands.
The gusts of wind, swirling with sand, lashed against my skin, filling me with a raw, untamed energy that sent a thrill through me.

I raised my hand, and the sky responded—a massive thundercloud began to gather, rolling and surging ominously.
I gazed at the desert illuminated by flashes of lightning, feeling not a shred of fear.

"Let it pour! This time, I will master the power of Rain!"

Raindrops pounded the sand, darkening it with each fall, creating a somber symphony over the endless desert.

I had come here seeking to harness the Mantra—the very essence of rain. I dreamed of breaking through my limits and transforming this barren land into something vibrant.
Was that naive? Perhaps.

Yet, reality often proves harsher than our dreams. Despite the rain's relentless assault, the desert showed little sign of change. My powers felt insignificant, merely a small patch stitched onto an endless wasteland.

Exhausted, my limbs felt as heavy as stone. I forced myself to blink, trying to dispel the dizziness that clouded my mind.
Though I hadn't fully mastered the Mantra, I had grasped the limits of my abilities.
A twinge of disappointment lingered, but I had no regrets. Without trying, I would never have known.

Just as I was about to withdraw my power, I spotted a tiny black dot in the distance—no larger than a sesame seed—moving toward me.
I blinked again, ensuring it wasn't a mirage. As it drew closer, I recognized a weary traveler.
He dragged himself forward, barely able to stay upright.

Before I could utter a word, he tilted his head back, his cracked lips parting as he greedily gulped the rainwater around him.
After a moment, he managed a hoarse, grateful thank you.
"I... dropped my compass and lost my way. Just when I thought I was done for, I saw those rain clouds above you."
"Whether it was a mirage or not, I had to take the gamble. I never thought... I'd survive. Guess luck was on my side..."
"You saved me... Words can't express my gratitude."

Was this mere chance, or was my luck somehow reaching out to him?

I couldn't dwell on it any longer. All I felt was a fire igniting in my heart, burning brighter than any previous moment of breakthrough.
A sudden warmth flared at my waist, and runes that had lain dormant for years illuminated, reflecting my growth.

A single act of kindness had brought an unexpected reward.
Everything Fon had learned—her growth, her resolve, her courage—fell upon her heart like gentle raindrops, deepening her understanding of the world and herself, nurturing the seed of "epiphany."

After grasping the Mantra, Fon didn't choose the conventional path to return to her family and continue her cultivation.
From the traveler she encountered in the Scorching Sands, she heard about Catto City for the first time.
"Maybe I should go check it out!" True to her heart, she set her sights on a new destination, drawn toward a much larger world.

Since her last leap from great heights, Fon had become addicted to the exhilarating rush of unbounded freedom.
Upon arriving in Catto City, she joined an extreme sports club.
Her glider traced graceful arcs in the sky as she leaped into the blue, charting new trajectories among the clouds.

In her new life, Fon noticed that those around her seemed to absorb little bits of her good luck.
This brought her immense joy.
Perhaps there was a hidden cost to fate's abundance, but Fon had no qualms about sharing these "gifts."
Even if it meant she would have to pay the price.

The moon peered through the clouds, painting the wet streets in silver.
Two "rats" splashed through alleyway puddles, their escape frantic and uncoordinated.

"Darn it! Since when did that girl know?"
"Shut your mouth! Just run! If she catches us—"
The flat of a blade cracked against their faces with surgical precision, sending them sprawling like discarded puppets.

"I'm sorry! I was wrong—Ah!"
A scream tore through the slums' night sky. No lights flickered on behind the windows.
Here, survival meant looking the other way.

I was busy teasing a stray cat when the leader finally arrived.
His eyes locked onto the two traitors pinned to the ground—blades speared through their calves—and he swallowed hard.
"Apologies, Miss. We... fell behind."
"They're all yours. Drag them back and let 'Don' handle the questioning."
"Understood. Also... the boss wanted you to have this."
He offered a wax-sealed envelope, its center stamped with a white orange blossom.

"A letter from my sister?"
I snatched it, already turning away.
"Clean this up. And don't bother me today—unless the city's burning down."
"Yes, Miss."

The frustration bled away, replaced by the crisp scent of citrus.
It had been too long since her last letter. Not since my birthday.
But what could I expect? She had her "family duties" overseas, and I had my hands full here...
Enough to make your skull throb.

"Once I'm of age, I'll visit her myself!"
"Wonder if that 'Catto City' she wrote about is half as dazzling as she claims..."
Back then, I was still naive enough to dream.
Dream of trading Shyriitrik's endless rain for sunlit citrus groves.
Of laughing with her like we did as children.

The rain in Shyriitrik arrived without warning—just like the old Don's sudden departure.
Now, the question of who would hold the family together had every boss on edge.
The mansion's air hung thick with tension, the scent of gunpowder clinging to every breath.

Tonight, the storm raged harder than usual. Thunder rolled between the drumming raindrops against the windows, a relentless clatter that refused to let me sleep.
Wide awake, I threw on my coat and stepped into the hallway, hoping the night air might clear my head.

Bang!
The crack of gunfire woke the estate, its echo chased by pounding footsteps down halls.
"Move! Alert the boss! We're under attack!"
No time to think. I snatched up my blade and sprinted toward the chaos.

"Hurry! The boss wants no survivors!"
"Behind you! It's a Felinian!"
"Take down the one with the blade first!"
"Ah—!"
Screams and the metallic tang of blood filled the corridor, thick enough to taste.
Sixty? Sixty-two? I lost count.
The manor's architecture became my weapon as I dealt with each traitorous "family" member in turn.
Bullet after bullet found its mark, until my body was more holes than flesh.
My strength bled out with each passing second, until even standing became impossible.

Then—a hand seized my wrist, yanking me toward the back door.
"Miss! This way!"
Bullets hissed past my ears. The butler's voice cut through the smoke.
"Go to Catto City. Find your sister. And never come back."
"Let go! What happens to the family if I leave?!"
"It's the boss's orders!"

The mansion burned behind me, its flames twisting in the rain like some tragic opera.
Gunfire. Screams. War cries. That endless storm—all of it blending into a single, bloody crescendo.
My ruined body finally gave out, forcing my retirement from this crimson spectacle.

And just like that... I left my "family" behind. I left my home behind.

Catto City was everything a bustling metropolis should be.
Shyriitrik was all smoke, liquor, and bullets—this place? A rare moment of peace.
But sightseeing was the last thing on my mind. The fate of my family gnawed at me like an open wound.

In my first few days, I discreetly asked around, hoping to uncover any news about them.
Yet whenever I brought up the "Camorra Family," people either play dumb or avoid my gaze.
For a family of our standing, this silence was baffling... A cold suspicion settled in my gut.
The public library's archives might hold the answers I desperately sought.

"Search: Current address of the Camorra Family."
"Search results for 'Camorra Family address': one thousand entries found."
The screen flooded with entries, but my eyes zeroed in on the top one—a newspaper clipping from years ago:

Camorra Family Estate destroyed in tragic fire. The manager and the majority of the household perished. Several members are still unaccounted for.
The missing persons list was filled with too many familiar names...
My uncle, who never left home without his silk ties... My aunt, who patiently taught me piano scales... and... my sister...

"No. This... this can't be right!"
I slammed my fist against the console. The sharp pain did nothing to dull the harsher truth.
"Who would dare strike at our family? Didn't anyone from Shyriitrik investigate?"
"And my sister's letter... I'd recognize her handwriting anywhere!"
Rage, confusion, and betrayal all morphed into useless tears that streaked down my face.

"Property currently quarantined due to hazardous P-value levels. Affiliated orphanage now under Catto City jurisdiction."
The terminal's emotionless voice droned on, reciting facts I could no longer comprehend.
"Under Naka's supervision, the facility has been relocated to Southport and rebranded as the Stray Cat Shelter."

So... where did that leave me now?

The hot water poured over my skin, and I tilted my face upward, finally surrendering to the warmth I'd been craving for days.
All the grief and exhaustion I'd carried since leaving home melted away in those steaming rivulets.
For the first time since that terrible night, my shoulders actually relaxed.

A soft knock at the wooden door, accompanied by a slender silhouette on the frosted glass.
"Sorry, nothing fits perfectly. This will have to do for tonight."
"Thanks."
A bundle of blue fabric slid beneath the door. The nightgown was delicate, with an oversized bow stitched to the chest.
It was probably the closest thing she could find to my size, though it looked like something meant for a schoolgirl.

When I emerged, the girl motioned me toward a chair.
"Storm's letting up. We'll get your clothes dried soon."
"..."
My response was a quiet nod, both hands wrapped around the cup as tangerine warmth filled the air.

I had gone to what remained of my family's estate today. Just like the newspapers said—nothing but skeletal walls and memories crumbling to dust.
With my last shred of hope, I trudged through the rain to this Stray Cat Shelter.
No familiar faces. No leads on my sister's whereabouts.
Just this stranger who had taken pity on a soaked stray at her doorstep.

"You... don't have anywhere to go, do you?"
Her question hung carefully in the air between us.
She was right. No family. No home. Just another alley cat with nowhere left to run.
What now? Book passage back to Shyriitrik and paint the streets red with vengeance?
Or dig deeper into Catto City's shadows to learn what really happened that night?

"Stay with us. Consider this your home."
The light rain ceased its patter against the window, making way for shy sunlight.
That offered hand... The way the golden light framed it... for a heartbeat, I saw different fingers.

"What should I call you?"
"Call me Anna."

On the Stray Cat Shelter's bookshelf sat a photo album with slightly frayed corners—a treasury of precious memories.
Anna ran her fingertips across its cover, the well-worn texture instantly familiar.

Sunlight poured through the window, illuminating the photographs.
The first page held a candid shot. There she was: pajama-clad, her expression unguarded in ways only sleep permits.

"Mmmph... Five more minutes..."
Ignoring Anna's sleepy protests, Raphaella persisted with a damp washcloth.
"If I don't drag you out of bed, you'll sleep till noon. Honestly, which of us is the older sister here?"
"Raphaella..."
"You've got me there..."

Anna's smile deepened as she turned the page.
The composition was clear: her blade-wielding form dominated the foreground, protecting the kids while scattered gang caps told the story of a hasty retreat.

"What's wrong? Tough enough to pick on kids but too scared to face me?"
"You'll pay for this!"
The children's cheers seemed to echo across time.
On the photo's back, a date and childish scrawl read: [Anna's our hero!]

Page after page, her life unfolded.
Ordinary moments that had become extraordinary memories.
Until the final photograph.
The Stray Cat Shelter family portrait. She remembered that terrible day—Jane and Raphaella kidnapped, Marie ready to charge into danger alone until she and the Inspector intervened.
"Troublesome little sisters... but I got you all home safe."

"Anna! Come play!"
A child's voice shattered her reverie. Anna gazed through the window. Raphaella pushed a cart overflowing with cat food while Jane and Marie weeded the garden.
The children waved enthusiastically, their smiles brighter than the afternoon sun.

"On my way!"
Anna closed the album gently and sprinted toward the waiting light.

The same nightmare again...
The dream always began the same way—my father dragging me into that warehouse.

What had I done to deserve this?
I could never remember. Maybe I had spilled my drink at dinner. Or perhaps I had cried after scraping my knee.

"Listen closely, Marie."
His fingers tangled in my hair, cold enough to send shivers down my spine.
"You're your mother's treasure. No one gets to ruin that. Do you understand?"

I stared into his hollow eyes—like looking at a ghost trapped behind glass.
"You'll stay here and think about what you've done. Won't you?"

Time stood still in that warehouse. It just... pooled. I curled tighter into the corner, numb to how long I'd been there.
Sometimes, I wondered if I even existed anymore.
Maybe I never had. Perhaps that was why he locked me away—to erase me. First from his memory. Then from mine. Then from the world.

If I wasn't a mistake, why did my mother die because of me?
If I were so precious, why did everyone look at me like I was something rotten?
If I were lucky, why wouldn't the pain just STOP?!

The questions spiraled until exhaustion consumed me.
The darkness felt warm then, as if nothing could hurt me.

When I woke, voices clashed around me—shocked, disgusted.
"The warehouse... It's still standing! The fire didn't touch it!"
"That girl—! She's alive! Surviving a blaze like that... Some luck."
"Tch. That curse of hers. Killed her mother, now her father."

I felt myself ascending, the clamor of humanity fading beneath me like a receding tide.
Some alchemy transformed me into a corvid spirit, dark wings carving circles over my homeland.
The fire had consumed my house. Taken my father. Spat me back out.

Below, my relatives huddled around the flames, debating my miraculous survival between curses.
I wanted to scream. To fight. But my beak could only produce a rasping caw—
Just like the storybook siren my mother once read to me—the one that summoned storms.

I always remembered that day from my childhood when the Chieftain took me out to fly a kite.
We ran across the open field, laughing as the wind lifted it higher and higher until it was just a speck against the clouds.
Then, without warning, the string snapped. The kite vanished into the horizon, swallowed by the sky.

I cried until my throat burned, sobbing that I was a monster—that I had cursed it. But the Chieftain merely rested a hand on my head and murmured something gentle...

What had he said?
I couldn't recall.

Maybe, after the fire, I had become that kite—cut loose, with nowhere to land.
The villagers' fearful stares chased me away, herding me deeper into isolation. Numbness settled in, followed by the wandering—restless, endless.

Days blurred together. I woke in ditches, alleyways, places where no one glanced my way. I learned to avoid crowds, to keep moving.
Fear followed me in some eyes, while others' gazes held only predatory calculation.
I was their prey—captured, caged, left to rot.
Was this punishment? I couldn't tell.

The ship's hold swallowed us whole—a cargo of the strange and unwanted, chained together.
Amidst the groans of the hull, I caught whispers—someone had paid for my capture.

Who? Who would want a jinx like me?
Before I could learn his name, a storm swept in and set me loose.
Was this fortune or fate? I didn't know anymore.

For a time, I dared to believe my wandering days were finally behind me.
Reaver City—they called it a sanctuary for lost souls like mine.

But monsters don't belong anywhere.
The curse clinging to my shadow poisoned everyone who came near.
Even among fellow outcasts, I remained untouchable.

Just this once... I allowed myself to believe that maybe I could finally find some peace.

The squad shunned me like plague carriers—all but their leader, who laughed at curses and shrugged off bad luck.
That easy smile of his never faltered as he referred to it as my "gift."
Yes, he called my misfortune a "gift."
A gift? I couldn't process it.

But that smile—so bright it burned away skepticism.
Fear could break me, but his calm words rebuilt something stronger.

He insisted that my abilities were being wasted, and by aligning with him, I could unlock incredible power—
A force of devastation for his enemies.

That look—I'd seen it before in my father's eyes. A pleasant mask over something primal and terrifying.
Flames danced behind my eyelids again. I was that terrified child once more, choking on smoke and despair.
The fire had never really died. It just found new ways to burn.
With the crows wheeling overhead, was another sign of disaster approaching?
Maybe they were right. Maybe I was the cursed creature that brought only ruin.

I didn't know.
But the truth didn't matter anymore.
Run, Marie.
Just run.

Running was what I did best. I fled from the stares that trailed me like shadows. I slipped through the grasping hands of hunters. Each stride took me further from those eyes—greedy, terrified, resentful.

But I wasn't just running from them; I was escaping the curse coiled around my bones.
If I couldn't stop the bad luck I carried, at least I could outpace the damage it left in its wake.

The leader's shouts pursued me as I fled. My misfortune, ever loyal, didn't spare him.
He stumbled over empty air, got tangled in wind-tossed debris, and even took a flowerpot to the skull like some slapstick punchline.
Soon, his curses faded behind me.

It was as if the curse, too, couldn't keep up.
For the first time, nothing followed. No hungry stares. No creeping dread.
Had I outrun the curse itself, or was this just another twist of fate? I didn't know.
But it felt like a victory.

Now... where to go?
The mercenaries' voices echoed in my memory.
"City of hope? Gah! All that glitter, and they'd still treat us like gutter trash."
"Even Reaver City's crime lords mind their manners in Catto City."
Their feigned scorn couldn't hide the longing beneath. It painted a vivid picture of that city in my mind.

Alone, I made my way to Catto City, creeping in from the sea before arriving in Southport.
I fell into a deep sleep in an empty alley.

In my dreams, I felt a sense of security I had never known before.
For once, the nightmares stayed away. A peace I had never experienced enveloped me.

The Chieftain's words, lost for so long, surfaced at last.
"Don't cry, little one. Luck's just testing you."

The warmth grew sharper.
Hmm? What's that... really pleasant fragrance?

My vision cleared, and I realized a Felinian girl was holding me.
Most Felinians have perky ears, but hers draped softly over her hair, and her voice was soothing like her touch.
"Hey, you're awake! How are you feeling? Any pain? When was the last time you ate? Just tell me what you need."

Marie had spent her whole life mastering one skill: running.
She ran from the shadow of her curse—and just as quickly from any hand that reached out to help.
In a quiet corner of Southport, she thought she'd finally found a place where no one would reach her. But when she opened her eyes, there it was: a meal, carefully prepared by that Scottish Fold Felinian Girl.

Marie could tell she was different from anyone she'd met before. There was no judgment in her, no hidden agenda—just warmth, like sunlight melting away the shadows.
Maybe, for now, it was safer to let Marie hide until she learned how to be around people.

For once, she didn't run—her differences wouldn't force her into solitude anymore.
The old terror had lessened its grip. Marie didn't know if Luck favored her, but she'd cheated fate once—wasn't that enough?

No longer the frightened child hidden in darkness, she was taking trembling but determined steps forward.
Whatever came next—storms or sunshine—would be hers to face.
She knew there would be more stumbles ahead, but there would also be hands reaching back. People who stayed.

The crows still circled above, their watchful eyes never leaving her. But Marie remembered the old tales now:
Sirens weren't omens of doom. They were simply misunderstood spirits, their clear eyes reflecting the hearts of those who gazed upon them.

Meet them with malice, and malice they would return.
But offer them kindness, and they would shed their ragged cloaks. In their true form, they would sing—sweet melodies of joy and blessings for those who approached with honest hearts.

Maybe Marie wasn't the one being tested—she was the challenge others had to face.

Morning light filtered through the curtains—another perfect day for everyone except me.
I lay motionless as the Pathos Particles in the air needled my skin. What sustained other Felinians felt like acid coursing through my veins.

The difference became obvious early on. While my peers tumbled joyfully through the Pathos Particle-thick air, I hid in shadowed corners, flinching at every breath.
The physician called it "hyper-sensitivity to Pathos Particles," a rare innate "affliction" among our kind.

"Erowyn, it's time for your medicine."
Mother's voice was soft beyond the door.
With trembling limbs, I took the emerald brew. The liquid coated my tongue with a sharp bitterness, but the relief was worth it.

Beyond my window, sunlight danced. Children shrieked with laughter, their joy agitating the Pathos Particles until my skull throbbed in time with their play.
"Why just me?"
The sheets twisted in my clenched fists.
It was torture—seeing the world through glass I could never break.
Here's the cruel joke: without Pathos Particles, I'd waste away.
With them, every moment burned.

Trapped between death and pain, I had no answers.
Then everything changed.

"Erowyn... how are you feeling today?"
Father sat by my bedside, a weighty tome of tales in hand, his voice gentle with concern.
"Same as usual..."
My voice barely carried.
"Want me to read you something? Maybe that adventure story you like?"
"Okay..."
When I'm stuck in bed year after year, unable to even see the outside world, my parents' voices reading stories become my lifeline.
The dazzling magic, the creeping shadows, the call of the abyss, the hero's adventures...
For those precious moments, I could escape my broken body and visit places where pain wasn't the only thing that felt real.

"...And though the hero now wielded a sword that could cleave mountains, the power came at a price—unbearable isolation, betrayal from those he trusted most... The energy ravaged his body, burning through him like wildfire day and night..."
Something clicked in my foggy brain at those words: power that burns.
"Dad—stop!"
I pushed myself upright so quickly that my vision swam. The room looked different somehow—sharper, clearer.
"You're saying... his power hurt him because it was too much?"
Dad smiled gently as he carefully explained things in simple terms.
"That's how every hero's story works, sweetheart. The greatest strengths always come with the hardest tests."
"Oh my god, Dad! That's me! This pain... it's not just sickness—it's a sign! I'm meant for something bigger!"

"Huh... What?"
Father blinked, then smiled gently.
"Well... I suppose you could see it that way."

My foggy mind suddenly cleared, thoughts racing faster than ever before—
Weak body? That just means I have a special magical constitution—powerful magic but a delicate vessel!
Constant pain? That's the shadow forces testing me—I must find a way to seal their source!
In that moment, something awakened within me. No longer was I a pitiful sickly kitten—I was a chosen one of destiny!
"Then it's settled—!" I stood on my bed, stretching my arms triumphantly toward the ceiling.
"I hereby declare myself the Great Demon Overlord!"

"Demon... Overlord?"
Mom walked in carrying breakfast, her face a perfect picture of bewilderment.
"Exactly!" I lifted my chin proudly.
"Those painful Pathos Particles? They must be the work of evil demons! And I—I will master them all! One day, they'll bow to my will!"
My parents exchanged glances, then turned back to me, their expressions caught between laughter and tears.
"Now that you've made your choice, you must see it through to the end, dear!"
"Erowyn's compassion will conquer the evil Pathos Particles—the world will be safe!"

That fateful day marked my rebirth—I, Erowyn, became the "Demon Overlord."
And whenever the pain returned, I reminded myself—this is merely the trial before my true power awakens!

The moment I declared myself the "Demon Overlord," fate finally started to work in my favor.
It all began during one of my worst, pain-filled nights. I woke up screaming from nightmares, only to see a towering figure in the shadows.
"That scent... pure Abyss energy. Remarkable that a kitten could withstand such torment."
"I am NO kitten! I am Erowyn, the future Demon Overlord!"
"My mistake."
Minotara looked exactly how a supreme overlord should—radiating piercing stares and regal bearing, though her expression softened just a fraction when she looked at me. 
"I am Minotara, Keeper of the Abyss. Thine... ally."
Her grip sent black flames swirling across my palm. "Awakening your latent power," she explained.
"Minotara! Mark me well—I shall root out the knave who scattereth these Pathos Particles and fulfill mine glorious destiny!"
"Any clues yet?"
"Pah! None dare show their face before my radiance! Yet... I have caught a whiff of their scent!"
I declared with complete conviction.

Of course, fate loves throwing curveballs.
Since Minotara awakened the Abyss within me, I have walked among mortals—and even attended their school.
But their "Pathos Technology" lessons struck me like a thunderbolt:
"Pathos Particles are fundamental to nature's fabric—"
"Nature's... work?" Can it be?
Mine archfoe is... Nature itself?
No! This has to be a trick! Mortals see only the surface—the true villain lurks deeper still!
Though mine mission now hid in shadow, my resolve to save this world never wavered.

Then came my big break. Mine unique constitution drew the eye of Pathos Technology's scholars.
With my family's blessing, I became their most esteemed research subject.
"Erowyn, your samples are invaluable to our work. Thank you for your cooperation!"
The senior researcher gave me formal recognition following the successful assessment.
"Hark! To serve mine 'World Salvation' is thine honor! Hasten thy research against 'Pathos Pollution'—lest I intervene and render thee obsolete!"
A look of quiet pride crossed the researcher's face as he repeatedly nodded in agreement.
"Absolutely! We're doubling our efforts!"
With these mortal researchers at my command, victory was practically guaranteed!
Mwahahaha! Try as I might, I couldn't keep the triumphant grin off my face.

Erowyn noticed the occasional strange looks and smirks from passersby—but she didn't care.
She had something better now: her own devoted following of lovable street cats.

Their first meeting had been an accident.
One rainy evening during her "royal patrol," a bony little kitten darted out of an alley.
"Darest thou, lowly creature, disturb mine august presence—?"
The kitten's big, pleading eyes stopped her mid-sentence.
She fished some treats from her pocket and crouched down.
"Since thou dost humbly petition... I deign to bestow mine bounty."
The kitten snatched the treat, rubbed against her leg, then—with constant purring and backward glances—led her to the Stray Cat Shelter.
Dozens of hungry eyes blinked up at her from the shadows.

Something inside Erowyn shifted. She straightened up, adopting her most commanding voice.
"Hark! I, Erowyn, Demon Overlord, do proclaim this domain under mine protection! Let all feline-kind here gathered be counted as mine subjects! To thee I pledge peace and provender!"
As ever, she spoke with lofty airs— a tiny orange kitten headbutted her hand, purring like an engine.
Before she knew it, she was gently scratching behind its ears.

"Fie... A clowder of mewling vassals..."
She murmured, unable to suppress a smile.
"So be it! Since thy faith in mine is so absolute, I shall establish here a temporary court, and with mine might, carve out for thee a kingdom!"

The lonely girl who had invented a grand title to survive her pain had finally found a tangible realm where she truly belonged.
No longer adrift in imagination, she anchored herself in the care of these small creatures. Responsibility, unexpected yet kind, became the bridge between her and a life she could embrace.

"Mom, am I doing this move right?"
Sunlight streamed through the window, warming the wooden floor. I twirled barefoot, my skirt fluttering like the waves.

"Very graceful, sweetheart."
Mom set down her fishing net, her eyes shining with pride.
"Lift your arms a little higher, like a seabird taking flight—that's it, just like a petrel."

I adjusted my pose, practicing the dance again and again.

"Wonderful! You're getting better every day, Beatrice."
"Of course! This year, I'll perform for everyone at the summer festival!" I announced, excitement bubbling over.
"I'll dance for the sea, and wish for every fishing boat to come back full every single day!"

At that moment, Dad walked in, laughing heartily.
"Our little princess is going to put on a show? I'll have to prepare my loudest applause!"
"Applause isn't enough," Mom chimed in, "I'll make you the prettiest dress for your performance."

"Yay! A new dress!"
I spun across the floor, my heart full of anticipation for the festival.

Back then, I could never have imagined that beautiful summer would become a nightmare I'd never escape.

The festival night had finally arrived.
The beach was alive with color, laughter, and joy—every corner sparkled with vibrant decorations.
The night market was a whirlwind of excitement; children and adults mingled at every stall, savoring summer snacks and playing delightful games. Beneath the canopies, the elders watched the festivities with gentle, contented smiles.
Clutching my parents' hands, I darted through the crowd.
"Beatrice~ Come try Aunt Marie's famous fried fish balls!"
"They're delicious!" I said, biting into a hot fish ball and inhaling sharply from the heat. "Aunt Marie, you're the best!"
"You little rascal, slow down!" Aunt Marie laughed, handing me another skewer. "Don't fill up too much—you've got to perform later!"
"Aunt Marie, you'll come watch my performance, right?"
"Of course! As soon as I finish this batch, I'll be at the stage, cheering you on!"

"Mom, Dad—this way, the stage is just ahead!"
The time for my performance was near. I ran ahead, waving eagerly back at my parents.
"—Ah!"
I tripped and crashed into a snack cart, tumbling to the ground.
When I stood up, I saw my beautiful dress was stained with all sorts of food and sauce.
"What am I going to do… my dress… it's ruined…"
"It's alright, sweetheart, don't cry… Mommy will clean it up," Mom said gently.
"No stain could ever hide the fact that you're our little princess," Dad added, smiling as they both tried to wipe away the mess.

"The next performer… Beatrice! Please get ready to go on stage!"
The host's voice echoed, and panic washed over me.
Looking down at my dirty dress, thinking of all those expectant faces, I made the most timid choice of my life—
I pushed my parents aside and ran, away from the stage and into the night.

I ran all the way to the little hill behind the village, sinking down in sadness.
Below, the festival still sparkled with lights, laughter drifting up with the wind. On stage, other children were performing, and waves of applause rose and fell from the crowd.

"Mom… Dad… you must be disappointed in me…"
I hugged my knees to my chest, tears streaming down my face.
After all those days of practice, after all their excitement, I just ran away… Now they're probably searching everywhere for me. They must be so worried, and so let down…

As I drowned in guilt, a strange sound reached my ears.
I looked up toward the sea, past the festival grounds. Under the moonlight, the ocean's calm surface twisted with eerie light. Dark waves gathered and swelled at an unnatural speed.

"What… is that?"
Wiping away my tears, I stood up, unease crawling through me.
Before I could react, a monstrous tide of black water surged toward the shore—toward the festival.

"Everyone, run! The black tide is coming!"
In an instant, celebration turned to chaos.
People scattered in panic, children cried, adults shouted names into the night.

"Beatrice—! Beatrice, where are you—!"
My parents' voices cut through the chaos. They were fighting against the fleeing crowd, desperately searching for me.

"Dad! Mom! I'm here!" I shouted, running down the hill as fast as I could.
But it was too late.

The black tide devoured everything in its path, swallowing the festival in seconds.
I watched, powerless, as my parents' figures were lost to the darkness.

"No! No! Dad! Mom!"
The tide surged up the hill toward me.
I tried to run, but slipped—falling into a deep pit.

Darkness swallowed me whole.

"…Stay awake… Don't fall asleep…"
Somewhere in the haze, a voice whispered in my ear.

"So noisy…"
I tried to open my eyes, but my eyelids felt impossibly heavy.

"She's still alive… Hurry…"
The voices faded in and out. I wanted to answer, but I couldn't make a sound.

"So tired… Just let me rest a bit longer…"

I don't know how long I slept.
When I finally opened my eyes—
White. Everything was white. White ceiling, white walls, white bedsheets. The air smelled faintly of disinfectant.

Where was I? Where were Mom and Dad?
Memories flooded back—
The festival, the black tide, my parents disappearing into the darkness—

"Ah—!"
I screamed in terror.
"Dad! Mom!"
Curled up on the bed, I shook all over.

"Sweetheart! Oh, sweetheart—"
A nurse in white hurried in, grabbing my hand.
"It's alright, you're safe now…"
"Where are Mom and Dad?" I clung to her, shaking her arm desperately.

Her expression changed—sad, gentle.
She didn't answer. Instead, she took out a mask for me to breathe through.
"Here, take a deep breath. This will help you feel better."

Cool air filled my lungs, and drowsiness washed over me.
I fought to keep my eyes open, but darkness crept in.
Just before I slipped away, I saw the pity in the nurse's eyes.
In that look, I understood the truth I never wanted to face.

My tears soaked the pillow in silence.

The sun rose and set, day after day.
But Beatrice remained trapped in that endless, sorrowful night.

She spent her days in the garden of the Emotional Care Center, silent and unmoving, watching flowers bloom and fade. The nurses understood: this child's heart was still lost in that summer night.

Five years passed in a blur.

Then one day, a visiting group came to the center, bringing small gifts for each child.
That night, as always, Beatrice couldn't sleep. She sat up in bed, her eyes falling on the gift box beside her.
She opened it mechanically, like a puppet. Inside was a picture book about summer festivals.
The cheerful cover felt like a beautiful, endless void, drawing her in.
Page after page, children danced on stage, adults cheered below, and the night market's lights lit up every smiling face…

"…Uu… Uu…"
Five years' worth of grief burst from her in uncontrollable sobs.
"Ah… ahhh—!"

A soft, eerie voice drifted in from the window.
"Hehe… poor thing, haunted by such lovely memories…"
A masked figure stood outside, their voice like something from a dream.

"Do you want to see them again? …Your parents."
Beatrice looked up, eyes blurred with tears, meeting the gaze of this strange visitor.

"If you hold a summer festival—one that grants everyone's wishes—you'll see them again."
Reason told Beatrice this was impossible, but longing made her voice tremble: "R…really?"

"Of course. Your sadness, your regret, your longing… are such powerful things."
With a wave of the masked figure's hand, black particles of emotion poured from Beatrice's chest, weaving themselves into a beautiful dress—just like the one she wore back then.

"Put it on. Go on—bring the festival back to life."
"Invite everyone. Gather their wishes, their happiness…"

"Wishes… happiness…" The masked figure's words echoed in her mind. Light returned to Beatrice's eyes. "A festival… If I can make everyone's wishes come true… then everyone will come… and so will Mom and Dad…"

At midnight, Beatrice stood before the mirror, dressed in a gown woven from pain and longing. She smiled, but tears still lingered at the corners of her eyes.

She would finish the performance she never completed.
She would try to heal the regret that could never truly fade.

But what awaited her—redemption from the past, or simply another dream from which she could never wake?

I'll never forget that moment.
With my only student—and staunchest supporter—Cauvin as witness, I cut my own oxygen and took the final step: uploading my mind.

When my breathing stopped, I saw it—the boundless ocean of information.
In an instant, the city unfurled before me.

The first wave of EMC devices and smart terminals wasn't large, yet billions of circuits lit up.
A torrent of data slammed into me; the city dissolved—then reassembled.

I saw—
Live status for every subway line; patient records from Emotional Intervention Centers; wind and humidity from weather stations; reservoir levels; school attendance; every library book; Council vote tallies…
